    Secrets --> Integrations
    Secrets --> Plugins
    Integrations --> External
    API --> Streams
    Streams --> Domain
    API --> Audit
    Domain --> Audit

docs.title: Trust Boundaries
docs.text:
Primary trust boundaries:

  1. Browser or API client to ChannelForge
  2. Reverse proxy to ChannelForge
  3. ChannelForge to Media Sources
  4. ChannelForge to plugin runtime
  5. ChannelForge to managed filesystem
  6. ChannelForge to SQLite
  7. ChannelForge to backup destination
  8. Public output clients to stream and artifact endpoints
  9. Webhook senders to webhook ingress
  10. Host operating system to container
  11. Package source to plugin installer
  12. Imported file to import pipeline

Every boundary requires explicit validation and authorization.

docs.title: Identity Assets
docs.text:
• Password verifiers
  • Session tokens
  • API tokens
  • Setup token
  • Recovery credentials
  • Role assignments
  • Permission grants

docs.title: Integration Assets
docs.text:
• Plex tokens
  • Jellyfin API keys or tokens
  • Emby API keys or tokens
  • Provider cookies
  • Provider client certificates
  • Provider transcode credentials
  • Path mappings
  • Internal addresses

docs.title: Plugin Assets
docs.text:
• Plugin package
  • Signature metadata
  • Plugin secret values
  • Permission grants
  • Plugin state
  • Network allowlists
  • Publisher trust records

docs.title: Editorial Assets
docs.text:
• Network Profiles
  • Programming Configuration
  • Schedule Plans
  • Approval records
  • Publication pointers
  • Templates
  • Programming Packs

docs.title: Runtime Assets
docs.text:
• Stream tokens
  • Active session control
  • FFmpeg command plans
  • Source access descriptors
  • HLS segments
  • Runtime diagnostics
  • Hardware reservations

docs.title: Persistence Assets
docs.text:
• SQLite database
  • Managed files
  • Backups
  • Audit records
  • Migration state
  • Encryption key material

docs.title: Threat Actors
docs.text:
Potential threat actors include:

  • Unauthenticated internet user
  • Unauthenticated local-network user
  • Authenticated low-privilege user
  • Compromised administrator session
  • Stolen API token holder
  • Malicious plugin publisher
  • Compromised plugin package source
  • Malicious or compromised Media Source
  • Malicious webhook sender
  • Malicious imported configuration
  • Compromised reverse proxy
  • User with filesystem access
  • User with Docker host access
  • Malware on the host
  • Supply-chain attacker
  • Accidental operator

docs.title: Threat Categories
docs.text:
ChannelForge security must address:

  • Credential theft
  • Session hijacking
  • Brute-force authentication
  • Privilege escalation
  • Cross-site request forgery
  • Cross-site scripting
  • Server-side request forgery
  • Command injection
  • SQL injection
  • Path traversal
  • File upload abuse
  • Plugin escape
  • Secret leakage
  • Log leakage
  • Backup leakage
  • Unauthorized stream access
  • Unauthorized runtime control
  • Schedule tampering
  • Publication tampering
  • Provider impersonation
  • Webhook replay
  • Denial of service
  • Dependency compromise
  • Package tampering
  • Downgrade attacks
  • Data corruption
  • Insecure restore
  • Audit deletion or forgery

docs.title: Security Zones
docs.text:
Suggested logical zones:

  • Public output zone
  • Authenticated management zone
  • Elevated administration zone
  • Integration zone
  • Plugin zone
  • Persistence zone
  • Backup zone
  • Host zone

Security controls vary by zone.

docs.title: Management API Default
docs.text:
The Management API is authenticated by default.

Unauthenticated access is limited to:

  • Liveness
  • Initial setup bootstrap under strict conditions
  • Public output endpoints explicitly enabled
  • HDHomeRun-compatible discovery if enabled
  • Webhook endpoints with provider-specific verification

docs.title: Public Output Default
docs.text:
XMLTV, M3U, and live streams should not be public by default.

Instance policy may enable:

  • Local-network access
  • Signed token access
  • API-token access
  • Reverse-proxy authentication
  • Public access

Public access requires explicit confirmation and warning.

docs.title: Authentication Model
docs.text:
Version 1 supports:

  • Browser sessions
  • Scoped API tokens
  • Initial setup token
  • Optional trusted reverse-proxy authentication

Future versions may support:

  • OIDC
  • Passkeys
  • MFA
  • Client certificates

docs.title: User Identity
docs.text:
Every user has a ChannelForge-owned User ID.

Authentication identifiers include:

  • Username
  • Optional email
  • API token prefix
  • Reverse-proxy subject

User identity is not derived from display name.

docs.title: Username Requirements
docs.text:
Username policy must define:

  • Length
  • Allowed characters
  • Case normalization
  • Uniqueness
  • Reserved names
  • Change policy

Username comparison should be normalized and deterministic.

docs.title: Password Authentication
docs.text:
Password authentication requires:

  • Strong password hashing
  • Per-password salt
  • Configurable work factor
  • Constant-time comparison
  • Rate limiting
  • Generic failure messages
  • Secure password reset or administrator reset
  • Password change invalidation policy

docs.title: Password Hashing
docs.text:
Use a modern password-hashing function.

Preferred classes:

  • Argon2id
  • scrypt
  • PBKDF2 only when required by platform constraints

Plain fast hashes are prohibited.

Prohibited examples:

  • MD5
  • SHA-1
  • Unsalted SHA-256
  • Reversible encryption as password storage

docs.title: Password Hash Parameters
docs.text:
Parameters must be:

  • Versioned
  • Stored with verifier
  • Upgradeable
  • Tuned for deployment class
  • Bounded against memory exhaustion

docs.title: Password Rehash
docs.text:
On successful login, if parameters are outdated:

  • Rehash with current parameters
  • Replace verifier atomically
  • Preserve session
  • Record security event only if policy requires

docs.title: Password Policy
docs.text:
Version 1 should favor length over complex character rules.

Policy may include:

  • Minimum length
  • Maximum length
  • Block known breached passwords where feasible
  • Reject username-equivalent passwords
  • Permit password managers
  • Permit spaces and Unicode
  • Avoid forced periodic expiration without cause

docs.title: Password Input Handling
docs.text:
Passwords:

  • Are never trimmed silently
  • Are never logged
  • Are never included in validation echoes
  • Are accepted only over protected transport where remote access is used
  • Are cleared from transient UI state where practical

docs.title: Login Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Login attempts are rate-limited by:

  • Source address classification
  • Username key
  • Instance-wide threshold
  • Token bucket or equivalent policy

Rate limiting must avoid permanent account denial by attackers.

docs.title: Login Failure Message
docs.text:
Use a generic message such as:

Authentication failed.

Do not reveal whether:

  • Username exists
  • Account is disabled
  • Password is wrong
  • Role is insufficient

Detailed reason may be recorded internally.

docs.title: Login Lockout
docs.text:
Hard lockout is optional.

A safer default may use:

  • Progressive delay
  • Temporary cooldown
  • Rate limiting
  • Security alert after threshold

Permanent lockout requires administrator recovery.

docs.title: Browser Session
docs.text:
A browser session includes:

  • Session ID
  • User ID
  • Created timestamp
  • Last activity
  • Expiration
  • Authentication strength
  • Revocation state
  • Client metadata summary
  • Token hash or server-side opaque reference

docs.title: Session Token
docs.text:
Session tokens must be:

  • Cryptographically random
  • High entropy
  • Opaque
  • Unpredictable
  • Stored only as a secure hash where server-side storage is used
  • Rotated after authentication state changes where appropriate

docs.title: Session Cookie
docs.text:
Recommended cookie attributes:

  • HttpOnly
  • Secure when HTTPS is used
  • SameSite=Lax or stricter according to UI needs
  • Narrow path
  • No Domain attribute unless required
  • Bounded lifetime

docs.title: Session Expiration
docs.text:
Policies may include:

  • Idle timeout
  • Absolute timeout
  • Remember-me timeout
  • Administrative maximum
  • Reauthentication requirement for sensitive actions

docs.title: Session Rotation
docs.text:
Rotate session identity after:

  • Login
  • Privilege elevation
  • Password change
  • Role change where applicable
  • Security-sensitive account change

docs.title: Session Revocation
docs.text:
Session revocation may occur after:

  • Sign out
  • Password reset
  • User disable
  • Administrator revocation
  • Suspicious activity
  • Token theft report
  • Backup restore into new instance policy

docs.title: Session Listing
docs.text:
Users should be able to view active sessions with:

  • Approximate client
  • Created time
  • Last activity
  • Address classification
  • Current session indicator

Sensitive fingerprinting details should be minimized.

docs.title: Reauthentication
docs.text:
Sensitive actions may require recent authentication.

Examples:

  • Create administrator
  • Change password
  • Rotate encryption key
  • Restore backup
  • Purge plugin
  • Disable authentication
  • Enable public access
  • Export sensitive diagnostics

docs.title: API Tokens
docs.text:
API tokens provide non-browser access.

A token includes:

  • Token ID
  • Owner
  • Prefix
  • Secret hash
  • Scopes
  • Created timestamp
  • Expiration
  • Last used timestamp
  • Revocation
  • Description

docs.title: API Token Secret
docs.text:
The full token is shown only at creation.

ChannelForge stores:

  • Secure hash
  • Identifying prefix
  • Metadata

docs.title: API Token Entropy
docs.text:
Tokens must have sufficient random entropy.

Do not use:

  • Sequential IDs
  • UUID alone as secret
  • User-chosen secrets
  • Reversible encrypted token values unless operationally required

docs.title: API Token Scope
docs.text:
Scopes must be least-privilege.

Suggested high-level scopes:

  • catalog:read
  • catalog:write
  • networks:read
  • networks:write
  • schedules:generate
  • schedules:approve
  • schedules:publish
  • runtime:read
  • runtime:control
  • sources:read
  • sources:write
  • plugins:read
  • plugins:manage
  • backups:read
  • backups:manage
  • audit:read
  • admin

docs.title: API Token Expiration
docs.text:
Tokens should support expiration.

Long-lived tokens require explicit confirmation.

docs.title: API Token Revocation
docs.text:
Revocation is immediate for new requests.

Cached authorization must not outlive revocation beyond a short bounded interval.

docs.title: API Token Display
docs.text:
The UI may display:

  • Prefix
  • Description
  • Owner
  • Scopes
  • Created
  • Expires
  • Last used
  • Revoked

It must not display the original secret.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Initial setup is a privileged bootstrap phase.

It must prevent arbitrary remote users from claiming the instance.

docs.title: Setup States
docs.text:
Suggested states:

  • UNINITIALIZED
  • SETUP_IN_PROGRESS
  • INITIALIZED
  • RECOVERY_REQUIRED

docs.title: Setup Token
docs.text:
A setup token may be provided through:

  • Console output
  • Environment variable
  • Mounted secret
  • Local file readable by administrator
  • Localhost-only bootstrap page

docs.title: Setup Token Requirements
docs.text:
The setup token must be:

  • High entropy
  • Single use
  • Time bounded or initialization bounded
  • Removed or invalidated after setup
  • Never logged after initial controlled display
  • Not stored in browser history where avoidable

docs.title: Remote Setup
docs.text:
Remote setup should require explicit deployment configuration.

Default setup may be limited to:

  • Localhost
  • Local subnet under warning
  • Console-confirmed token

docs.title: First Administrator
docs.text:
Initial setup creates the first administrator.

The operation must be atomic.

docs.title: Setup Completion
docs.text:
After setup:

  • Setup endpoints are disabled.
  • Setup token is invalidated.
  • Administrator session is established.
  • Audit begins.
  • Security posture is summarized.
  • Insecure configuration warnings are shown.

docs.title: Setup Recovery
docs.text:
Recovery may require:

  • Host filesystem access
  • Console command
  • Mounted recovery secret
  • Backup restore

A network-only unauthenticated reset endpoint is prohibited.

docs.title: Authorization Model
docs.text:
Authorization is role- and permission-based.

It may include resource-state checks.

docs.title: Authorization Decision
docs.text:
An authorization decision considers:

  • User or token
  • Role assignments
  • Token scopes
  • Resource
  • Command
  • Resource state
  • Plugin permission context
  • Deployment policy
  • Recent reauthentication where required

docs.title: Roles
docs.text: Suggested built-in roles:

docs.title: Administrator
docs.text:
Can:

  • Manage users
  • Manage security
  • Manage Media Sources
  • Manage plugins
  • Manage backups
  • Approve and publish schedules
  • Control runtime
  • Read audit
  • Configure public access

docs.title: Program Director
docs.text:
Can:

  • Manage Networks
  • Manage Channels
  • Manage programming configuration
  • Generate schedules
  • Review schedules
  • Approve schedules where policy permits
  • Publish schedules where granted

docs.title: Operator
docs.text:
Can:

  • Read Networks and schedules
  • Read runtime status
  • Restart Channels
  • Enter maintenance mode
  • View operational diagnostics
  • Start approved jobs

docs.title: Read Only
docs.text:
Can:

  • Read authorized resources
  • View status
  • Export non-sensitive reports where granted

docs.title: Viewer
docs.text: May access limited first-party viewing surfaces if implemented.

docs.title: Permission Families
docs.text:
Suggested permission families:

  • Instance
  • Users
  • Security
  • Media Sources
  • Catalog
  • Networks
  • Channels
  • Programming
  • Scheduling
  • Approval
  • Publication
  • Runtime
  • Plugins
  • Backups
  • Audit
  • Diagnostics
  • Output access

docs.title: Permission Examples
docs.text:
• INSTANCE_READ
  • INSTANCE_MANAGE
  • USER_READ
  • USER_MANAGE
  • SECURITY_MANAGE
  • MEDIA_SOURCE_READ
  • MEDIA_SOURCE_MANAGE
  • CATALOG_READ
  • CATALOG_MANAGE
  • NETWORK_READ
  • NETWORK_MANAGE
  • CHANNEL_READ
  • CHANNEL_MANAGE
  • PROGRAMMING_MANAGE
  • SCHEDULE_GENERATE
  • SCHEDULE_APPROVE
  • SCHEDULE_PUBLISH
  • RUNTIME_READ
  • RUNTIME_CONTROL
  • PLUGIN_READ
  • PLUGIN_MANAGE
  • BACKUP_READ
  • BACKUP_MANAGE
  • AUDIT_READ
  • DIAGNOSTICS_READ
  • OUTPUT_ACCESS

docs.title: Role Assignment
docs.text:
Role assignment requires:

  • Administrator permission
  • Expected user version
  • Audit
  • Optional reauthentication
  • Prevention of accidental last-administrator removal

docs.title: Last Administrator Protection
docs.text:
The system must prevent:

  • Disabling the last active administrator
  • Removing the last administrator role
  • Archiving the last administrator

Recovery requires explicit host-level procedure.

docs.title: Permission Evaluation
docs.text:
Permission checks must occur:

  • At route boundary
  • In application service
  • At plugin broker boundary
  • At sensitive repository or secret boundary where defense in depth is useful

docs.title: Authorization Failure
docs.text:
Authorization failure returns:

  • 403 or concealed 404
  • Stable error code
  • Request ID
  • No sensitive resource details

docs.title: Service Accounts
docs.text:
Version 1 may represent automation through API tokens owned by users.

Dedicated service accounts may be added later.

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Protection
docs.text: A user cannot grant permissions they do not possess unless Administrator policy explicitly allows delegated administration.

docs.title: Secret Categories
docs.text:
Secret categories include:

  • Password verifiers
  • Session token hashes
  • API token hashes
  • Media Source credentials
  • Plugin secrets
  • Webhook secrets
  • Backup encryption keys
  • Signing private keys
  • Stream signing keys
  • Cookie signing keys
  • Recovery secrets

docs.title: Secret Storage Model
docs.text:
Secrets are stored through a Secret Service.

The Secret Service provides:

  • Create
  • Read for scoped operation
  • Rotate
  • Revoke
  • Delete where safe
  • Metadata
  • Audit
  • Encryption
  • Key versioning

docs.title: Secret Reference
docs.text:
Domain records store a Secret Reference.

A Secret Reference includes:

  • Secret ID
  • Category
  • Owner type
  • Owner ID
  • Created timestamp
  • Rotated timestamp
  • Revocation state
  • Key version
  • Metadata

It does not contain plaintext.

docs.title: Encryption at Rest
docs.text:
Reusable credential values should be encrypted at rest.

Examples:

  • Plex token
  • Jellyfin token
  • Emby token
  • Plugin API key
  • Webhook signing secret
  • Backup destination credential

docs.title: Password Verifiers
docs.text: Password verifiers are hashed, not encrypted.

docs.title: API Token Values
docs.text: API token secrets are hashed when verification can use one-way comparison.

docs.title: Encryption Key
docs.text:
A master key or key-encryption key must not be stored unprotected beside the encrypted database values it protects.

Possible sources:

  • Environment variable
  • Mounted secret file
  • Container secret
  • Host keyring
  • External secret service

docs.title: Key Material Requirements
docs.text:
Key material must be:

  • High entropy
  • Correct length
  • Versioned
  • Access restricted
  • Excluded from logs
  • Excluded from backups unless explicitly protected
  • Available for restore

docs.title: Key Hierarchy
docs.text:
A possible hierarchy:

  • Master key
  • Data-encryption keys by version
  • Per-secret nonce
  • Authenticated encryption metadata

Exact cryptographic construction is deferred.

docs.title: Authenticated Encryption
docs.text:
Secret encryption must provide:

  • Confidentiality
  • Integrity
  • Nonce safety
  • Versioning
  • Associated data binding where appropriate

Unauthenticated encryption is prohibited.

docs.title: Associated Data
docs.text:
Associated data may bind ciphertext to:

  • Instance ID
  • Secret ID
  • Owner type
  • Owner ID
  • Secret category
  • Key version

docs.title: Encryption Metadata
docs.text:
Stored metadata includes:

  • Algorithm version
  • Key version
  • Nonce
  • Ciphertext
  • Authentication tag where separate
  • Created timestamp

docs.title: Key Rotation
docs.text:
Key rotation workflow:

  1. Introduce new active key version.
  2. Continue decrypting old versions.
  3. Encrypt new secrets with new version.
  4. Re-encrypt existing secrets in bounded job.
  5. Verify.
  6. Retire old key only after completion.
  7. Record audit.

docs.title: Key Loss
docs.text:
If the encryption key is lost:

  • Encrypted secrets cannot be recovered.
  • Catalog and schedule data may remain readable.
  • Media Sources require credential reentry.
  • Plugin secrets require reentry.
  • Encrypted backups may be unrecoverable.

This must be documented clearly.

docs.title: Secret Rotation
docs.text:
Secret rotation should not require deleting the owning resource.

Examples:

  • Rotate Plex token
  • Rotate plugin API key
  • Rotate webhook secret
  • Rotate stream signing key

docs.title: Secret Revocation
docs.text:
Revoked secrets:

  • Cannot be read for new operations
  • Remain in audit metadata
  • May remain encrypted until retention cleanup
  • Trigger dependent health findings

docs.title: Secret Access Logging
docs.text:
Secret values are not logged.

Access metadata may include:

  • Secret ID
  • Owner
  • Operation
  • Request ID
  • Plugin ID
  • Timestamp
  • Outcome

High-frequency access may use aggregated metrics rather than full audit.

docs.title: Secret Redaction
docs.text:
Redaction must cover:

  • Authorization headers
  • Cookies
  • Query tokens
  • Signed URLs
  • Password fields
  • API key fields
  • Provider tokens
  • Private keys
  • Secret JSON fields
  • Environment variables marked secret

docs.title: Redaction Strategy
docs.text:
Use structured redaction by field and context.

Do not rely only on regular expressions after string formatting.

docs.title: Media Source Credentials
docs.text:
Media Source credentials are scoped to one Media Source.

An adapter receives them only for:

  • Connection test
  • Synchronization
  • Artwork access
  • Playback resolution
  • Health check

docs.title: Provider Token Exposure
docs.text:
Provider tokens must not appear in:

  • Management API responses
  • M3U
  • XMLTV
  • Channel logos
  • Client stream redirects
  • Audit details
  • FFmpeg logs
  • Error messages

docs.title: Provider URL Handling
docs.text:
Provider URLs may contain query credentials.

They must be:

  • Held in restricted runtime structures
  • Redacted before logging
  • Not persisted as canonical identity
  • Not returned to clients
  • Expired according to provider policy

docs.title: Local File Credentials
docs.text:
Path access may rely on host permissions rather than explicit credentials.

ChannelForge still treats provider-reported paths as untrusted.

docs.title: Plugin Security
docs.text: Plugin security requirements from 10-plugins.md are mandatory.

docs.title: Plugin Trust Levels
docs.text:
Suggested trust levels:

  • Built-in trusted
  • Project signed
  • Trusted publisher
  • Locally approved unsigned
  • Development
  • Quarantined

docs.title: Plugin Permission Enforcement
docs.text: Plugin permissions must be enforced at runtime, not only installation.

docs.title: Plugin Secret Isolation
docs.text:
A plugin receives only secrets owned by:

  • Its Plugin Registration
  • Its Plugin Instance
  • An explicitly granted integration capability

docs.title: Plugin Network Isolation
docs.text:
Plugin outbound access is denied by default.

Approved access should use a broker with:

  • Host allowlist
  • Scheme allowlist
  • Port allowlist
  • Redirect restrictions
  • Timeout
  • Response-size limits
  • DNS and address validation
  • Redaction
  • Metrics

docs.title: Plugin Filesystem Isolation
docs.text:
Plugins use namespaced storage.

They cannot read:

  • SQLite database
  • Core secret files
  • Other plugin storage
  • Host paths
  • Managed media paths

unless a specific extension contract provides a controlled capability.

docs.title: Plugin Process Isolation
docs.text: External plugins should not run with unrestricted in-process access in production.

docs.title: Plugin Package Installation
docs.text: Package validation must occur before executable content runs.

docs.title: Plugin Supply Chain
docs.text:
Plugin package trust includes:

  • Signature
  • Publisher
  • Checksum
  • Source
  • Version
  • Advisory state
  • Permissions
  • Compatibility

docs.title: Plugin Quarantine
docs.text:
A quarantined plugin cannot:

  • Start
  • Register contributions
  • Run jobs
  • Access secrets
  • Access network
  • Serve routes

docs.title: Stream Authorization
docs.text:
Live Channel output may require:

  • Authenticated session
  • API token
  • Signed stream token
  • Local network policy
  • Reverse-proxy authentication

docs.title: Signed Stream Token
docs.text:
A signed stream token may include:

  • Token ID or nonce
  • Channel ID
  • Protocol
  • Audience
  • Issued time
  • Expiration
  • Optional client binding
  • Optional one-time state

docs.title: Stream Token Requirements
docs.text:
Tokens must be:

  • Signed with a dedicated key
  • Short lived
  • Scope limited
  • Revocable where practical
  • Excluded from logs
  • Avoided in referrer leakage
  • Avoided in browser history where possible

docs.title: Query Token Risk
docs.text:
When clients require query tokens:

  • Use short expiration
  • Redact query string
  • Use no-referrer policy
  • Avoid embedding on third-party pages
  • Prefer path or header alternatives where client compatibility permits

docs.title: Stream Token Rotation
docs.text: Stream signing keys support versioning and overlap.

docs.title: Local Network Access
docs.text:
A local-network policy may authorize requests by address range.

This is weaker than authenticated access.

Warnings must explain:

  • VPN exposure
  • Wi-Fi guest access
  • Reverse-proxy bypass
  • Container network behavior
  • IPv6 exposure

docs.title: XMLTV and M3U Access
docs.text:
Artifact access policies may differ from live stream access.

Possible modes:

  • Authenticated
  • Static access token
  • Signed URL
  • Local network
  • Public

docs.title: Artifact Access Token
docs.text:
A static artifact token should be:

  • Revocable
  • Rotatable
  • Scoped
  • High entropy
  • Hidden from logs

docs.title: HDHomeRun-Compatible Security
docs.text:
Some HDHomeRun-compatible clients assume unauthenticated local access.

When enabled:

  • Restrict to trusted interfaces or networks where possible.
  • Warn about exposure.
  • Avoid embedding provider credentials.
  • Advertise only intended Channels.
  • Limit tuner capacity.
  • Keep management API protected.

docs.title: Discovery Security
docs.text:
UDP discovery can reveal:

  • Device identity
  • Base URL
  • Channel availability
  • Host address

Discovery should be configurable by interface.

docs.title: Runtime Control Security
docs.text:
Runtime control commands require elevated permission.

Examples:

  • Restart Channel
  • Stop session
  • Force source
  • Enter maintenance
  • Exit maintenance
  • Change tuner count
  • Change public output

docs.title: Schedule Integrity
docs.text:
Editorial state transitions require:

  • Authentication
  • Authorization
  • Optimistic concurrency
  • Validation
  • Audit
  • Immutable approved records

docs.title: Approval Separation
docs.text:
An instance may optionally require separate people for:

  • Authoring
  • Approval
  • Publication

Version 1 may support this through permissions, even if not mandatory.

docs.title: Publication Protection
docs.text:
Publication requires:

  • Approved Plan
  • Expected current publication
  • Authorized actor
  • Idempotency
  • Audit
  • Optional reauthentication

docs.title: Runtime Versus Editorial Separation
docs.text:
Operational recovery cannot silently change:

  • Programming Configuration
  • Approved Schedule Plan
  • Approval record
  • Publication history

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text: Cookie-authenticated mutation endpoints require CSRF protection.

docs.title: CSRF Defenses
docs.text:
Potential defenses:

  • SameSite cookies
  • Synchronizer token
  • Double-submit token
  • Origin checking
  • Referer checking as supplemental control
  • Custom header for same-origin requests

docs.title: CSRF Token
docs.text:
A CSRF token must be:

  • Session bound
  • Unpredictable
  • Compared safely
  • Required for mutation
  • Excluded from logs

docs.title: Origin Validation
docs.text:
For browser mutations, validate:

  • Origin
  • Trusted host
  • Scheme
  • Proxy trust

Missing Origin behavior must be deliberate.

docs.title: Bearer Tokens and CSRF
docs.text:
Bearer tokens in Authorization headers are not automatically sent by browsers across origins.

They do not use cookie CSRF semantics, but CORS and XSS remain relevant.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text: CORS is disabled by default for management APIs.

docs.title: Allowed Origins
docs.text:
Allowed origins must be:

  • Explicit
  • Scheme-specific
  • Host-specific
  • Port-specific
  • Validated

Wildcard origins with credentials are prohibited.

docs.title: CORS Methods
docs.text: Allow only required methods.

docs.title: CORS Headers
docs.text: Allow only required request headers.

docs.title: Preflight Caching
docs.text: Preflight caching should be bounded.

docs.title: XSS
docs.text:
The first-party web interface must prevent cross-site scripting.

Controls include:

  • Contextual output escaping
  • Safe templating
  • Sanitized rich text
  • Content Security Policy
  • No unsafe HTML from providers
  • No direct rendering of plugin strings as HTML
  • No executable uploaded files
  • Safe URL schemes

docs.title: Provider Text
docs.text:
Provider metadata is untrusted.

Descriptions, titles, tags, and filenames must be escaped in UI.

docs.title: Markdown or Rich Text
docs.text:
If Markdown is supported:

  • Sanitize output
  • Disable raw HTML by default
  • Restrict links and images
  • Apply safe URL policies

docs.title: Content Security Policy
docs.text:
The web UI should use a Content Security Policy.

It should restrict:

  • Script sources
  • Style sources
  • Frame ancestors
  • Object sources
  • Base URI
  • Form actions
  • Connections
  • Images

Plugin UI may require separate policy or sandboxing.

docs.title: Clickjacking
docs.text:
Administrative UI must prevent unauthorized framing.

Use:

  • frame-ancestors
  • Legacy header where needed

docs.title: MIME Sniffing
docs.text: Use X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff where applicable.

docs.title: Referrer Policy
docs.text: Use a restrictive Referrer Policy to avoid token leakage.

docs.title: Open Redirects
docs.text:
Redirect targets must be:

  • Local and allowlisted
  • Relative
  • Or validated against explicit trusted origins

docs.title: SSRF
docs.text:
Server-side requests are a major trust boundary.

Sources include:

  • Media Source URLs
  • Plugin network calls
  • Artwork URLs
  • Webhook callbacks
  • Metadata providers
  • Import references
  • Backup destinations

docs.title: SSRF Defenses
docs.text:
Controls include:

  • Scheme allowlist
  • Host validation
  • Port policy
  • DNS resolution checks
  • Redirect validation
  • Address classification
  • Cloud metadata blocking
  • Link-local blocking where appropriate
  • Loopback policy
  • UNIX socket prohibition
  • Response-size limits
  • Timeouts
  • No arbitrary user headers
  • Credential forwarding restrictions

docs.title: Local Network Exception
docs.text:
ChannelForge intentionally connects to local Plex, Jellyfin, and Emby servers.

Therefore SSRF policy must distinguish:

  • Approved configured Media Source
  • Arbitrary user-provided URL
  • Plugin-declared host
  • Artwork provider URL
  • Import reference

docs.title: DNS Rebinding
docs.text:
Where practical:

  • Resolve host before connection.
  • Validate resolved address.
  • Revalidate redirects.
  • Avoid forwarding credentials across host changes.
  • Use connection destination checks.

docs.title: Redirect Security
docs.text:
Redirect policy must prevent:

  • HTTPS downgrade
  • Credential forwarding to another host
  • Redirect loops
  • Excessive redirects
  • Redirect to disallowed address class

docs.title: HTTP Header Security
docs.text:
Custom headers are allowlisted by integration type.

Users cannot configure arbitrary headers that impersonate internal services.

docs.title: Command Injection
docs.text:
User input must not become shell command text.

FFmpeg invocation must use:

  • Argument arrays
  • Typed options
  • Allowlisted protocols
  • Validated filters
  • Managed paths

docs.title: Shell Execution
docs.text:
Core features should avoid shell invocation.

When unavoidable:

  • Use fixed executable
  • Use argument array
  • Never interpolate untrusted input into shell script
  • Bound environment
  • Record executable identity
  • Validate path

docs.title: FFmpeg Security
docs.text:
FFmpeg is a complex parser and network client.

Controls include:

  • Protocol allowlist
  • Input source validation
  • Output path control
  • Filter allowlist
  • Timeout
  • Process isolation
  • Resource limits
  • Updated build
  • No arbitrary user command fragments

docs.title: FFmpeg Protocols
docs.text:
Only required protocols should be enabled.

Potential allowed protocols:

  • File
  • HTTP
  • HTTPS
  • Pipe
  • Provider-specific safe protocols where required

Potentially dangerous protocols should be disabled unless justified.

docs.title: SQL Injection
docs.text:
All SQL uses parameter binding.

Prohibited:

  • Concatenating user input into SQL
  • Raw filter fragments from API
  • Plugin SQL
  • Provider-supplied column names
  • Arbitrary ORDER BY without allowlist

docs.title: Dynamic Sorting
docs.text: Sort fields map through an allowlist to fixed SQL expressions.

docs.title: Database File Protection
docs.text: The SQLite file must be protected by filesystem permissions.

docs.title: SQLite Security
docs.text:
Controls include:

  • Foreign keys enabled
  • Trusted schema policy
  • No arbitrary extension loading
  • Migration checksum validation
  • No user-supplied SQL
  • No public database download
  • Backup authorization

docs.title: Managed File Security
docs.text: Managed file paths are generated by ChannelForge.

docs.title: Path Traversal
docs.text:
Reject:

  • ..
  • Absolute paths
  • Drive paths where not allowed
  • UNC paths where not allowed
  • Encoded traversal
  • Null bytes
  • Symlink escapes
  • Case-collision ambiguity

docs.title: Symlinks
docs.text: Managed storage should avoid following untrusted symlinks.

docs.title: Upload Security
docs.text: Uploads are untrusted.

docs.title: Upload Controls
docs.text:
• Size limit
  • File count limit
  • MIME allowlist
  • Signature validation
  • Extension normalization
  • Safe filename
  • Image dimension limit
  • Decompression limits
  • Temporary storage
  • Checksum
  • Malware scanning policy where available
  • Non-executable serving

docs.title: Image Security
docs.text:
Image uploads may contain:

  • Parser exploits
  • Huge dimensions
  • Metadata leakage
  • Polyglot content
  • SVG scripts

SVG should be sanitized or disallowed for untrusted uploads.

docs.title: Archive Security
docs.text:
Plugin and import archives require:

  • Path traversal defense
  • Symlink defense
  • File count limit
  • Decompressed-size limit
  • Nested archive policy
  • Duplicate path detection
  • Case-collision detection

docs.title: Download Security
docs.text:
Downloads use:

  • Safe Content-Type
  • Safe Content-Disposition
  • No path exposure
  • Authorization
  • Audit for sensitive exports
  • Expiration for temporary bundles

docs.title: Temporary Files
docs.text:
Temporary files:

  • Use managed temp root
  • Use random names
  • Use restrictive permissions
  • Are cleaned after failure
  • Are reconciled after crash
  • Never become executable by default

docs.title: Backup Security
docs.text: Backups may contain the entire security state.

docs.title: Backup Confidentiality
docs.text:
Backup archives should be encrypted when they include:

  • Encrypted secret database values
  • User accounts
  • API token hashes
  • Network topology
  • Audit
  • Plugin state
  • Managed files

docs.title: Backup Encryption
docs.text:
Backup encryption must use:

  • Authenticated encryption
  • Versioned format
  • Strong key derivation for passphrase-based mode
  • Random salt
  • Integrity verification
  • No plaintext key inside archive

docs.title: Backup Passphrase
docs.text:
If passphrase-based encryption is supported:

  • Minimum strength
  • No logging
  • No storage unless explicitly configured
  • Confirmation
  • Recovery warning
  • Memory-hard key derivation

docs.title: Backup Destination Credentials
docs.text: Destination credentials are secrets.

docs.title: Backup Access
docs.text:
Only authorized users may:

  • Create
  • List
  • Download
  • Delete
  • Verify
  • Restore

docs.title: Backup Download
docs.text:
Backup download requires:

  • Recent authentication
  • Audit
  • No shared-cache storage
  • Safe filename
  • Optional one-time URL
  • Short expiration

docs.title: Restore Security
docs.text: Restore is a privileged destructive operation.

docs.title: Restore Controls
docs.text:
• Administrator permission
  • Recent authentication
  • Verified backup
  • Compatibility check
  • Confirmation
  • Pre-restore safety backup
  • Maintenance mode
  • Audit
  • No arbitrary archive extraction
  • Secret-key availability check

docs.title: Restore Trust
docs.text:
A backup from another instance may contain:

  • Users
  • API tokens
  • Plugins
  • Trusted publishers
  • Public access settings

Restore preview must show security impact.

docs.title: Cross-Instance Restore
docs.text:
Cross-instance restore may require:

  • New administrator confirmation
  • Token invalidation
  • Session invalidation
  • Stream key rotation
  • Provider credential revalidation
  • Plugin disablement

docs.title: Audit
docs.text: Security-relevant actions require audit.

docs.title: Audit Security Events
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Login success
  • Login failure threshold
  • Session revocation
  • Password change
  • API token creation
  • API token revocation
  • Role assignment
  • Last-administrator protection event
  • Setup completion
  • Public access enabled
  • Media Source credential rotation
  • Plugin installation
  • Unsigned plugin approval
  • Permission grant
  • Plugin quarantine
  • Backup download
  • Restore
  • Encryption key rotation
  • Security setting change
  • Diagnostic export
  • Repeated denied access
  • Provider identity mismatch

docs.title: Audit Record Integrity
docs.text: Audit records are append-only.

docs.title: Audit Content
docs.text:
Audit includes:

  • Actor
  • Action
  • Target
  • Time
  • Outcome
  • Request ID
  • Correlation ID
  • Reason
  • Prior and new version where applicable
  • Address classification
  • Authentication method

docs.title: Audit Redaction
docs.text:
Audit must not contain:

  • Password
  • API token
  • Session token
  • Provider token
  • Plugin secret
  • Backup passphrase
  • Private key
  • Full signed URL

docs.title: Audit Access
docs.text: Audit access requires elevated permission.

docs.title: Audit Retention
docs.text: Security audit retention should be long-lived.

docs.title: Audit Export
docs.text:
Audit export requires:

  • Permission
  • Bounded time range
  • Redaction
  • Audit of export
  • Safe temporary file

docs.title: Logging Security
docs.text: Logs are operational data and may be sensitive.

docs.title: Log Categories
docs.text:
• Application
  • Security
  • Integration
  • Plugin
  • Playout
  • Persistence
  • HTTP access
  • Audit

docs.title: Log Redaction
docs.text: Redact before serialization where possible.

docs.title: URL Logging
docs.text: Do not log full query strings when they may contain tokens.

docs.title: Header Logging
docs.text:
Never log:

  • Authorization
  • Cookie
  • Set-Cookie
  • Provider token headers
  • Plugin secret headers

docs.title: Body Logging
docs.text: Request and response bodies are disabled by default.

docs.title: Diagnostic Mode
docs.text:
Diagnostic mode may enable additional logging.

It must:

  • Warn administrator
  • Expire automatically
  • Preserve redaction
  • Limit duration and size
  • Avoid raw secret capture

docs.title: Log Retention
docs.text: Retention is bounded and configurable.

docs.title: Log Access
docs.text: Detailed logs require permission.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: ChannelForge should minimize personal data.

docs.title: Personal Data Examples
docs.text:
• Username
  • Email
  • Client address
  • Session metadata
  • Audit actor
  • Provider account identity
  • Viewing session metadata

docs.title: Data Minimization
docs.text:
Collect only what is necessary for:

  • Authentication
  • Authorization
  • Security diagnostics
  • Audit
  • Operation

docs.title: Client Address Handling
docs.text:
Client addresses may be:

  • Classified as local or remote
  • Truncated
  • Hashed for aggregation
  • Retained for limited time
  • Excluded from ordinary UI

docs.title: Viewing Data
docs.text: Version 1 should not build user viewing profiles unless explicitly required.

docs.title: Privacy and Plugins
docs.text: Plugins receive only minimum projections.

docs.title: Privacy and Diagnostics
docs.text: Diagnostic bundles must be redacted.

docs.title: Data Export
docs.text: User data export is not a primary version 1 requirement, but the system should make account and audit data identifiable for future support.

docs.title: Data Deletion
docs.text: Deleting a user may preserve audit identity through tombstone or pseudonymous reference.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text: Remote access should use HTTPS.

docs.title: TLS Termination
docs.text:
TLS may terminate at:

  • ChannelForge
  • Trusted reverse proxy

docs.title: Direct HTTP
docs.text:
Plain HTTP may be acceptable only on trusted local networks.

The UI should warn when:

  • Management access is remote over HTTP
  • Secure cookies cannot be used
  • API tokens may traverse plaintext
  • Public exposure is detected

docs.title: HSTS
docs.text: HSTS is appropriate only when the deployment is reliably HTTPS.

docs.title: Certificate Validation
docs.text: Outbound HTTPS validates certificates by default.

docs.title: Self-Signed Providers
docs.text:
A Media Source may explicitly trust:

  • Custom certificate authority
  • Specific certificate
  • Insecure TLS mode

docs.title: Insecure TLS
docs.text:
Insecure TLS mode:

  • Is source-specific
  • Is disabled by default
  • Requires warning and confirmation
  • Is auditable
  • Must not disable validation globally

docs.title: Reverse Proxy Trust
docs.text: Forwarded headers are trusted only from configured proxy addresses.

docs.title: Trusted Headers
docs.text:
Potential trusted headers:

  • Forwarded client address
  • Host
  • Scheme
  • Authenticated user
  • Request ID

docs.title: Header Spoofing
docs.text: Direct requests must not be able to inject trusted proxy identity headers.

docs.title: Host Validation
docs.text: The application validates Host and public URL construction.

docs.title: Proxy Authentication
docs.text:
Reverse-proxy authentication requires:

  • Explicit enablement
  • Trusted proxy address
  • Identity header
  • Header stripping at proxy
  • Direct-access policy
  • User mapping
  • Audit

docs.title: Direct Bypass
docs.text:
When proxy authentication is enabled, direct access must:

  • Be disabled, or
  • Ignore proxy identity headers, or
  • Require normal ChannelForge authentication

docs.title: Webhook Security
docs.text: Webhook payloads are untrusted.

docs.title: Webhook Verification
docs.text:
Possible verification:

  • Shared secret
  • HMAC signature
  • Provider token
  • Client certificate
  • Network allowlist
  • Replay timestamp
  • Event ID

docs.title: Webhook Body Limit
docs.text: Each webhook endpoint has a body limit.

docs.title: Webhook Replay
docs.text:
Use:

  • Event ID
  • Timestamp
  • Nonce
  • Payload checksum
  • Replay window

docs.title: Webhook Processing
docs.text:
Webhook requests:

  • Validate
  • Deduplicate
  • Queue work
  • Return quickly

They do not directly publish schedules or delete Catalog state.

docs.title: Unauthenticated Provider Webhook
docs.text:
Where provider lacks authentication:

  • Restrict network exposure
  • Rate limit
  • Treat as hint only
  • Verify through provider API
  • Never trust deletion event alone

docs.title: Denial of Service
docs.text: ChannelForge must bound expensive work.

docs.title: Request Limits
docs.text:
• Header size
  • Body size
  • Query length
  • Page size
  • Bulk count
  • Upload size
  • Archive size
  • Webhook size
  • Search complexity

docs.title: Background Work Limits
docs.text:
• Concurrent jobs
  • Per-source synchronization
  • Schedule generation concurrency
  • Plugin jobs
  • Backup jobs
  • Projection rebuilds
  • Artifact generation

docs.title: Runtime Limits
docs.text:
• Concurrent streams
  • Concurrent transcodes
  • Hardware encoder slots
  • Segment storage
  • FFmpeg process count
  • Per-client bandwidth where practical

docs.title: Resource Exhaustion
docs.text:
When capacity is exhausted:

  • Reject or queue new work
  • Preserve active sessions where policy prefers
  • Return explicit status
  • Avoid spawning unbounded processes

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Rate limits apply to:

  • Login
  • Setup
  • API token creation
  • Synchronization commands
  • Schedule generation
  • Backup
  • Restore
  • Diagnostics
  • Webhooks
  • Stream-token minting

docs.title: Rate Limit Storage
docs.text:
Rate-limit state may be in memory for version 1.

Security-critical limits should survive short restarts where practical.

docs.title: Abuse Detection
docs.text:
Potential detections:

  • Repeated login failures
  • Repeated denied permissions
  • Repeated invalid API tokens
  • Webhook flood
  • Plugin protocol violations
  • Stream-token abuse
  • Backup download anomalies

docs.title: Account Notification
docs.text:
Future versions may notify administrators about security events.

Version 1 should at least expose security findings.

docs.title: Security Findings
docs.text:
A Security Finding includes:

  • Finding ID
  • Severity
  • Category
  • Target
  • First observed
  • Last observed
  • Status
  • Evidence
  • Suggested action
  • Resolution
  • Audit reference

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Suggested levels:

  • INFO
  • LOW
  • MEDIUM
  • HIGH
  • CRITICAL

docs.title: Security Posture Checks
docs.text:
Potential checks:

  • Management exposed over HTTP
  • Public M3U enabled
  • Public stream enabled
  • Insecure TLS Media Source
  • Unsigned plugin enabled
  • Old backup
  • No recent backup
  • Encryption key missing
  • Weak setup state
  • Default administrator unchanged
  • Broad API token
  • Plugin broad network access
  • Reverse-proxy trust misconfigured
  • Discovery exposed on all interfaces

docs.title: Supply-Chain Security
docs.text:
ChannelForge depends on:

  • Application dependencies
  • Container base image
  • FFmpeg build
  • Plugin packages
  • Build pipeline
  • Release artifacts

docs.title: Dependency Management
docs.text:
Requirements:

  • Lockfile
  • Reproducible dependency resolution
  • Dependency review
  • Vulnerability scanning
  • Timely updates
  • Remove unused dependencies
  • Avoid unmaintained critical packages

docs.title: Release Integrity
docs.text:
Official releases should provide:

  • Version
  • Checksums
  • Signed release metadata where feasible
  • Changelog
  • Migration notes
  • Dependency provenance

docs.title: Container Image
docs.text:
Container images should:

  • Use minimal base
  • Run as non-root where feasible
  • Pin base version
  • Include only required tools
  • Avoid package managers in final layer where practical
  • Publish digest
  • Be scanned

docs.title: FFmpeg Supply Chain
docs.text: FFmpeg version and build source should be documented.

docs.title: Plugin Supply Chain
docs.text: Plugin packages require independent trust and permissions.

docs.title: Update Security
docs.text:
Application updates must:

  • Verify artifact integrity
  • Preserve backup
  • Run migrations safely
  • Avoid automatic downgrade
  • Record version change
  • Expose security notices

docs.title: Downgrade
docs.text:
Downgrade may be blocked when:

  • Database schema is newer
  • Security format changed
  • Plugin state incompatible
  • Secret encryption format incompatible

docs.title: Container Hardening
docs.text:
Recommended deployment controls:

  • Non-root user
  • Read-only root filesystem where practical
  • Writable mounted data directories only
  • Drop unnecessary Linux capabilities
  • No privileged mode
  • Limit devices
  • Limit memory and CPU
  • No Docker socket mount
  • No host PID namespace
  • No unnecessary host networking
  • Restrict outbound network where feasible

docs.title: Hardware Devices
docs.text:
Hardware transcode devices may require device access.

Grant only required devices.

docs.title: Docker Socket
docs.text: Mounting Docker socket into ChannelForge is prohibited for standard operation.

docs.title: Host Networking
docs.text:
Host networking may be needed for HDHomeRun discovery.

It increases exposure and must be documented.

docs.title: Filesystem Permissions
docs.text: Data directories should be owned by the configured application user.

docs.title: PUID and PGID
docs.text:
Where deployment supports PUID and PGID:

  • Use least-privileged IDs
  • Avoid root
  • Document media read access separately from data write access

docs.title: Read-Only Media Mounts
docs.text: Media mounts should be read-only where ChannelForge only needs playback.

docs.title: Backup Mounts
docs.text: Backup destination permissions should not grant unnecessary access to other host paths.

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
Recommended:

  • Keep management access restricted
  • Permit Media Source access
  • Permit client stream access
  • Restrict plugin destinations
  • Limit discovery interfaces

docs.title: IPv6
docs.text:
Security policy must account for IPv6 exposure.

Local-only IPv4 configuration does not imply IPv6 isolation.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text: Firewall rules are deployment responsibility, but ChannelForge should document required ports and protocols.

docs.title: Secret Environment Variables
docs.text:
Environment variables may expose secrets through:

  • Process inspection
  • Container inspection
  • Diagnostics

Mounted secret files are preferable where available.

docs.title: Secret File Permissions
docs.text:
Secret files should be:

  • Readable only by application user
  • Not served by web server
  • Outside plugin storage
  • Outside backup unless explicitly included

docs.title: Security Configuration
docs.text:
Security settings should include:

  • Session timeout
  • API token policy
  • Public output access
  • Trusted proxies
  • CORS
  • Allowed origins
  • Setup state
  • Plugin trust policy
  • Backup encryption policy
  • TLS warnings
  • Discovery interfaces
  • Rate limits

docs.title: Security Setting Changes
docs.text:
Changes require:

  • Appropriate permission
  • Expected version
  • Audit
  • Validation
  • Impact preview
  • Reauthentication for critical settings

docs.title: Secure Defaults
docs.text:
Default posture should be:

  • Authentication enabled
  • Public streams disabled
  • Public artifacts disabled
  • CORS disabled
  • Reverse-proxy auth disabled
  • Unsigned plugins disabled
  • Insecure TLS disabled
  • Outbound plugin network denied
  • Management diagnostics restricted
  • Setup token required
  • Backups recommended
  • No arbitrary filesystem paths
  • No arbitrary FFmpeg options

docs.title: Insecure Configuration Warning
docs.text: Warnings must be persistent until resolved or acknowledged.

docs.title: Security Headers
docs.text:
Management responses should use appropriate headers:

  • Content Security Policy
  • X-Content-Type-Options
  • Referrer-Policy
  • Frame restrictions
  • Cache-Control
  • HSTS when appropriate

docs.title: Cache Security
docs.text:
Sensitive responses use:

Cache-Control: no-store

docs.title: Artifact Cache Security
docs.text:
Public artifacts may be cached according to access mode.

Tokenized artifacts must avoid shared-cache leakage.

docs.title: Service Worker Security
docs.text:
If ChannelForge uses a PWA service worker:

  • Scope must be controlled
  • Sensitive API responses should not be cached
  • Logout should clear sensitive caches
  • Updates should not serve stale privileged UI indefinitely
  • Cache keys must not mix users

docs.title: Client Storage
docs.text: Avoid storing long-lived API tokens in browser localStorage.

docs.title: Clipboard
docs.text: The UI should minimize automatic clipboard exposure of secrets.

docs.title: One-Time Secret Display
docs.text:
When displaying a new API token:

  • Show once
  • Require explicit copy
  • Warn it cannot be recovered
  • Avoid analytics capture
  • Avoid logging
  • Clear from DOM on navigation where practical

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: Security errors must not reveal internals.

docs.title: Generic Internal Error
docs.text:
Unexpected errors return:

  • Stable code
  • Request ID
  • No stack trace
  • No SQL
  • No path
  • No secret
  • No raw provider response

docs.title: Security Error Codes
docs.text:
Suggested codes:

  • AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED
  • AUTHENTICATION_FAILED
  • SESSION_EXPIRED
  • SESSION_REVOKED
  • TOKEN_INVALID
  • TOKEN_EXPIRED
  • TOKEN_REVOKED
  • PERMISSION_DENIED
  • REAUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED
  • CSRF_VALIDATION_FAILED
  • ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED
  • RATE_LIMITED
  • SETUP_DISABLED
  • SETUP_TOKEN_INVALID
  • SECRET_UNAVAILABLE
  • SECRET_DECRYPTION_FAILED
  • INSECURE_CONFIGURATION_BLOCKED
  • PLUGIN_PERMISSION_DENIED
  • NETWORK_DESTINATION_DENIED
  • UPLOAD_REJECTED
  • BACKUP_VERIFICATION_FAILED
  • RESTORE_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED

docs.title: Incident Response
docs.text: ChannelForge should support a practical security incident workflow.

docs.title: Incident Categories
docs.text:
• Stolen session
  • Stolen API token
  • Media Source credential compromise
  • Plugin compromise
  • Backup leak
  • Encryption key compromise
  • Unauthorized publication
  • Unauthorized runtime control
  • Malicious webhook
  • Dependency vulnerability
  • Database theft
  • Host compromise

docs.title: Incident Actions
docs.text:
Potential actions:

  • Revoke all sessions
  • Revoke API tokens
  • Disable user
  • Rotate Media Source credential
  • Disable plugin
  • Quarantine plugin
  • Rotate stream signing key
  • Rotate cookie signing key
  • Rotate encryption key
  • Disable public access
  • Enter maintenance mode
  • Create backup
  • Export audit
  • Restore known-good backup
  • Preserve forensic logs

docs.title: Emergency Session Revocation
docs.text:
Administrators should be able to revoke:

  • One session
  • All sessions for one user
  • All noncurrent sessions
  • All sessions instance-wide

docs.title: Emergency Token Revocation
docs.text: Administrators should be able to revoke all API tokens.

docs.title: Emergency Plugin Disable
docs.text: A security command should disable all external plugins.

docs.title: Emergency Public Access Disable
docs.text:
A security command should disable:

  • Public streams
  • Public M3U
  • Public XMLTV
  • Discovery where configurable

docs.title: Forensic Preservation
docs.text:
After suspected compromise:

  • Preserve database copy
  • Preserve logs
  • Preserve audit
  • Preserve plugin packages
  • Preserve checksums
  • Avoid destructive cleanup before evidence capture

docs.title: Security Recovery
docs.text:
Recovery steps may include:

  1. Isolate host.
  2. Stop public access.
  3. Revoke sessions and tokens.
  4. Disable plugins.
  5. Rotate credentials.
  6. Review audit.
  7. Verify database integrity.
  8. Restore known-good backup if needed.
  9. Upgrade vulnerable components.
  10. Re-enable services gradually.

docs.title: Vulnerability Reporting
docs.text: The project should publish a security contact and disclosure process.

docs.title: Security Advisories
docs.text:
Advisories should include:

  • Affected versions
  • Severity
  • Impact
  • Mitigation
  • Fixed version
  • Migration or rotation steps

docs.title: Authentication Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Valid login
  • Invalid username
  • Invalid password
  • Disabled user
  • Expired session
  • Revoked session
  • Session rotation
  • Logout
  • Password change
  • Password rehash
  • Login rate limit
  • Setup token
  • Setup disabled after initialization

docs.title: API Token Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Valid token
  • Invalid token
  • Expired token
  • Revoked token
  • Missing scope
  • Prefix display
  • One-time secret display
  • Token rotation or recreation
  • Concurrent revocation
  • Last-used update
  • Rate limiting

docs.title: Authorization Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Every role
  • Every permission family
  • Route guard
  • Application-service enforcement
  • Resource-state enforcement
  • Last-administrator protection
  • Delegated permission limits
  • Concealed not found
  • Reauthentication requirement

docs.title: Secret Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Encrypt
  • Decrypt
  • Wrong key
  • Tampered ciphertext
  • Key version
  • Rotation
  • Revocation
  • Missing secret
  • Cross-owner access denial
  • Plugin isolation
  • Redaction
  • Backup and restore

docs.title: Session Security Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Cookie attributes
  • Idle timeout
  • Absolute timeout
  • Session fixation
  • Session rotation
  • Revocation
  • Password-change invalidation
  • User-disable invalidation
  • Concurrent sessions
  • CSRF

docs.title: CSRF Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Valid token
  • Missing token
  • Wrong token
  • Cross-session token
  • Invalid Origin
  • Same-site request
  • Bearer-token request
  • Preflight behavior

docs.title: CORS Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • No Origin
  • Allowed Origin
  • Disallowed Origin
  • Wildcard prohibited with credentials
  • Allowed methods
  • Allowed headers
  • Preflight
  • Reverse-proxy host behavior

docs.title: XSS Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Provider title containing HTML
  • Provider description containing script
  • Plugin label containing markup
  • Uploaded SVG
  • Markdown sanitization
  • URL scheme validation
  • CSP
  • Error message escaping

docs.title: SSRF Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Approved local Media Source
  • Arbitrary loopback
  • Link-local
  • Cloud metadata address
  • IPv6 loopback
  • DNS rebinding simulation
  • Redirect to private address
  • HTTPS downgrade
  • Cross-host credential forwarding
  • Plugin host allowlist
  • Oversized response
  • Timeout

docs.title: Command Injection Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • FFmpeg argument injection
  • Shell metacharacters
  • Filter injection
  • Filename injection
  • Environment injection
  • Plugin command attempt
  • Archive entry name

docs.title: SQL Injection Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Search query
  • Sort field
  • Filter
  • Provider metadata
  • Plugin proposal
  • Import file
  • Audit query
  • Raw JSON
  • Pagination cursor

docs.title: File Security Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Path traversal
  • Encoded traversal
  • Absolute path
  • UNC path
  • Symlink escape
  • Case collision
  • Null byte
  • Oversized file
  • MIME mismatch
  • Polyglot file
  • SVG script
  • Archive bomb
  • Interrupted upload
  • Temporary cleanup

docs.title: Plugin Security Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Invalid signature
  • Tampered package
  • Unsigned policy
  • Permission escalation
  • Cross-plugin secret access
  • Network denial
  • Filesystem denial
  • IPC fuzzing
  • Crash loop
  • Quarantine
  • Unsafe upgrade
  • Publisher revocation

docs.title: Stream Security Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Valid stream token
  • Expired token
  • Wrong Channel
  • Wrong protocol
  • Revoked key
  • Query token redaction
  • Local-network mode
  • Public mode warning
  • Concurrent abuse
  • Stream response cache headers

docs.title: Webhook Security Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Valid signature
  • Invalid signature
  • Replay
  • Duplicate event
  • Oversized payload
  • Unknown source
  • Unauthenticated provider mode
  • Rate limit
  • No direct state mutation

docs.title: Backup Security Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Encrypted backup
  • Wrong passphrase
  • Tampered archive
  • Missing key
  • Unauthorized download
  • Restore confirmation
  • Cross-instance security impact
  • Plugin trust restoration
  • Session invalidation
  • Token invalidation

docs.title: Reverse Proxy Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Trusted proxy
  • Untrusted proxy
  • Spoofed identity header
  • Spoofed Forwarded header
  • Host header
  • Scheme
  • Direct bypass
  • Public URL construction

docs.title: Supply-Chain Tests
docs.text:
Tests may cover:

  • Lockfile integrity
  • Dependency vulnerability threshold
  • Image scan
  • Release checksum
  • Plugin checksum
  • Migration checksum
  • Unsupported downgrade

docs.title: Property Tests
docs.text:
Useful properties:

  • A revoked session cannot authorize a new request.
  • A revoked API token cannot authorize a new request.
  • A user cannot grant permissions beyond allowed authority.
  • The last administrator cannot be removed accidentally.
  • Secret ciphertext modification causes decryption failure.
  • A plugin cannot access another plugin's secret.
  • A provider credential never appears in management responses.
  • A signed source URL never appears in ordinary logs.
  • A failed CSRF check causes no mutation.
  • A failed authorization check causes no mutation.
  • A failed optimistic concurrency check causes no mutation.
  • Public artifacts never contain provider credentials.
  • Stream tokens cannot authorize another Channel.
  • Redirects never forward credentials to an untrusted host.
  • Managed paths never escape configured roots.
  • Unsigned plugins cannot activate when policy prohibits them.
  • Quarantined plugins cannot execute.
  • Backup restore never activates unverified data.
  • Audit records contain no plaintext secrets.
  • Security configuration changes are auditable.

docs.title: Fuzz Testing
docs.text:
Fuzz targets should include:

  • JSON parsers
  • Plugin manifest
  • Plugin IPC
  • Webhook payloads
  • XMLTV import
  • M3U import
  • Archive extraction
  • Image metadata
  • Pagination cursors
  • Signed tokens
  • API validation

docs.title: Penetration Testing
docs.text:
Before broad release, test:

  • Authentication bypass
  • Authorization bypass
  • CSRF
  • XSS
  • SSRF
  • Command injection
  • SQL injection
  • File traversal
  • Plugin escape
  • Secret leakage
  • Backup exposure
  • Stream authorization
  • Reverse-proxy trust

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Suggested metrics:

  • Login success
  • Login failure
  • Login rate limit
  • Active sessions
  • Revoked sessions
  • API token usage
  • Permission denials
  • CSRF failures
  • CORS denials
  • SSRF denials
  • Plugin permission denials
  • Secret decryption failures
  • Webhook verification failures
  • Public stream requests
  • Backup downloads
  • Restore attempts
  • Security Findings by severity

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
Potential alerts:

  • Repeated administrator login failure
  • Repeated token failure
  • Repeated permission denial
  • Plugin quarantine
  • Secret decryption failure
  • Encryption key missing
  • Provider identity mismatch
  • Public access enabled unexpectedly
  • Backup verification failure
  • Restore attempt
  • Database integrity failure
  • Clock anomaly affecting token validation

docs.title: Clock Security
docs.text:
Token expiration and replay windows depend on accurate time.

ChannelForge must detect material clock changes.

docs.title: Clock Skew
docs.text:
Allow only bounded skew for:

  • Stream tokens
  • Webhook signatures
  • Session expiration
  • API token expiration

docs.title: Time Rollback
docs.text: A large backward clock change should create a security finding.

docs.title: Version 1 Required Behaviors
docs.text:
The version 1 security subsystem must:

  1. Require authentication for management APIs after setup.
  2. Support browser sessions.
  3. Support scoped API tokens.
  4. Use modern password hashing.
  5. Rate-limit login.
  6. Protect against session fixation.
  7. Support session revocation.
  8. Support API token revocation.
  9. Enforce server-side authorization.
  10. Protect the last administrator.
  11. Support recent reauthentication for critical operations.
  12. Store reusable credentials through encrypted secret storage.
  13. Keep encryption key separate from encrypted database values.
  14. Support key versioning.
  15. Support secret rotation.
  16. Redact secrets from logs, errors, and audit.
  17. Protect against CSRF.
  18. Restrict CORS by default.
  19. Escape untrusted UI content.
  20. Protect against SSRF.
  21. Protect against command injection.
  22. Use parameterized SQL.
  23. Protect managed file paths.
  24. Validate uploads and archives.
  25. Isolate plugins through permission brokers.
  26. Secure stream and artifact access.
  27. Verify webhooks or treat them only as hints.
  28. Encrypt or strongly protect backups.
  29. Audit privileged actions.
  30. Provide security findings and incident controls.
  31. Use secure defaults.
  32. Warn on insecure deployment choices.
  33. Support reverse-proxy trust configuration.
  34. Protect restore operations.
  35. Remain operable in one Docker container.

docs.title: Security Invariants
docs.text:
1. No management mutation occurs without authenticated authorization after setup.
  2. Passwords are never stored in plaintext.
  3. Passwords are never logged.
  4. Session tokens are unpredictable.
  5. API token secrets are shown only once.
  6. Revoked credentials cannot authorize new requests.
  7. The last administrator cannot be removed through ordinary commands.
  8. Reusable provider credentials are encrypted at rest.
  9. Encryption uses integrity protection.
  10. Encryption keys are not stored unprotected beside ciphertext.
  11. Secrets are excluded from ordinary API responses.
  12. Secrets are excluded from M3U and XMLTV.
  13. Provider signed URLs are not canonical identity.
  14. Provider credentials are not forwarded to unrelated hosts.
  15. CSRF failure causes no mutation.
  16. Authorization failure causes no mutation.
  17. Concurrency failure causes no mutation.
  18. CORS is not wildcarded with credentials.
  19. Untrusted metadata is escaped before UI rendering.
  20. User input does not become shell command text.
  21. SQL values are parameterized.
  22. Plugin packages execute only after validation.
  23. Plugin permissions are enforced at operation time.
  24. A plugin cannot read another plugin's secrets.
  25. Managed paths cannot escape storage roots.
  26. Backups are verified before restore.
  27. Restore requires elevated authorization and confirmation.
  28. Audit records do not contain plaintext secrets.
  29. Public output access is explicit.
  30. Stream tokens are Channel scoped.
  31. Webhook events do not directly mutate canonical state.
  32. Insecure TLS is source-specific and explicit.
  33. Trusted proxy headers are accepted only from trusted proxies.
  34. Direct proxy bypass cannot spoof authenticated identity.
  35. Security-critical configuration changes are auditable.
  36. Quarantined plugins cannot execute.
  37. Failed secret decryption does not return ciphertext or key details.
  38. Failed artifact generation does not remove prior valid artifact.
  39. Security incidents can revoke sessions and tokens.
  40. Version 1 remains local-first without assuming the LAN is trusted.

docs.title: Deferred Security Decisions
docs.text:
The following decisions remain open:

  • Exact password-hashing algorithm
  • Exact password-hashing parameters
  • Exact session storage design
  • Exact session cookie name
  • Exact session timeout defaults
  • Exact API token format
  • Exact API token scope matrix
  • Exact reauthentication interval
  • Exact CSRF mechanism
  • Exact Content Security Policy
  • Exact trusted-proxy configuration format
  • Exact reverse-proxy authentication header
  • Exact encryption algorithm
  • Exact key hierarchy
  • Exact key-storage mechanism
  • Exact key-rotation cadence
  • Exact backup encryption format
  • Exact backup passphrase KDF
  • Exact signed stream-token format
  • Exact stream-token expiration
  • Exact artifact access-token format
  • Exact rate-limit thresholds
  • Exact security finding workflow
  • Exact public-access warning flow
  • Exact self-signed certificate trust workflow
  • Exact plugin sandbox implementation
  • Exact plugin signature trust store
  • Exact vulnerability scanning pipeline
  • Exact container hardening profile
  • Exact IPv6 exposure defaults
  • Exact incident response UI
  • Exact MFA support
  • Exact OIDC support

docs.title: ChannelForge Deployment Specification
docs.text:
• Specification version: 0.1
  • Status: Draft
  • Last updated: 2026-07-27

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This document defines deployment architecture and operational requirements for ChannelForge version 1.

It specifies:

  • Supported deployment models
  • Docker image requirements
  • Docker Compose requirements
  • Unraid template requirements
  • Persistent storage
  • Configuration
  • Secrets
  • Networking
  • Reverse proxies
  • TLS
  • HDHomeRun-compatible discovery
  • Hardware acceleration
  • CPU and memory limits
  • Health checks
  • Startup
  • Shutdown
  • Migrations
  • Upgrades
  • Rollback
  • Backup
  • Restore
  • Logging
  • Observability
  • Security hardening
  • Release artifacts
  • Air-gapped operation
  • Troubleshooting
  • Support bundles
  • Operational runbooks

This document does not define:

  • Internal database schema
  • Public API field contracts
  • Schedule-generation algorithms
  • Plugin extension contracts
  • Exact user-interface behavior
  • Exact CI implementation
  • Exact cloud hosting products

Those concerns are defined in other architecture specifications.

docs.title: Deployment Mission
docs.text:
ChannelForge must be straightforward to install on a home server while remaining predictable, recoverable, and secure.

The supported deployment must:

  • Start from one documented container image
  • Preserve all durable state in mounted storage
  • Survive container recreation
  • Avoid requiring an external database
  • Support Docker Compose
  • Support Unraid
  • Support Plex, Jellyfin, and Emby connectivity
  • Support XMLTV, M3U, IPTV, and HDHomeRun-compatible output
  • Support optional hardware acceleration
  • Expose reliable health checks
  • Run as a non-root user where practical
  • Support backup and restore
  • Support controlled upgrades
  • Avoid hidden host dependencies
  • Produce actionable diagnostics

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Version 1 officially targets:

  • Docker Engine on Linux
  • Docker Compose
  • Unraid Community Applications-style template deployment
  • Single-container ChannelForge application
  • SQLite persistence
  • Managed local filesystem storage
  • Optional reverse proxy
  • Optional GPU or media-device access
  • Local network clients
  • Plex, Jellyfin, and Emby on the same or reachable networks

Version 1 may run in other environments, but they are not primary support targets unless documented.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
Version 1 does not require:

  • Kubernetes
  • Nomad
  • Docker Swarm
  • Multi-node active-active deployment
  • Managed cloud database
  • Distributed filesystem
  • Object storage
  • External message queue
  • Separate transcoder nodes
  • Windows service installation
  • macOS native service installation
  • Rootless-container support on every platform
  • High-availability failover
  • Automatic horizontal scaling

These may be considered later.

docs.title: Deployment Principles
docs.text:
1. Durable state lives outside the container image.
  2. The container is replaceable.
  3. SQLite remains local to supported storage.
  4. Startup performs validation before accepting normal traffic.
  5. Migrations are controlled and backed up.
  6. The application runs with least privilege.
  7. Device access is explicit.
  8. Network exposure is explicit.
  9. Public access is disabled by default.
  10. Health checks distinguish liveness from readiness.
  11. Backups are part of normal operation.
  12. Upgrades are reversible where schema compatibility permits.
  13. Logs go to standard output and managed files only when configured.
  14. Secrets are not embedded in images or Compose files by default.
  15. Unraid and Compose express the same architecture.
  16. Host networking is optional and justified only by discovery needs.
  17. Storage paths are documented and inspectable.
  18. Container restarts do not erase editorial state.
  19. Operators can identify the running application version.
  20. Support bundles redact secrets.

docs.title: Supported Topology
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Client["Plex / Jellyfin / Emby / IPTV Clients"]
    Proxy["Optional Reverse Proxy"]
    CF["ChannelForge Container"]
    Data["Persistent Data Volume"]
    Temp["Temporary Storage"]
    GPU["Optional GPU / Media Device"]
    Plex["Plex Server"]
    Jellyfin["Jellyfin Server"]
    Emby["Emby Server"]
    Backup["Backup Destination"]

    Client --> Proxy
    Proxy --> CF
    Client --> CF

    CF --> Data
    CF --> Temp
    CF --> GPU
    CF --> Plex
    CF --> Jellyfin
    CF --> Emby
    CF --> Backup

docs.title: Primary Deployment Unit
docs.text:
The primary deployment unit is one ChannelForge container.

It contains:

  • Web application
  • REST API
  • Scheduling engine
  • Integration adapters
  • Playout runtime
  • FFmpeg supervisor
  • SQLite client
  • Background Job workers
  • XMLTV and M3U generators
  • HDHomeRun-compatible HTTP service
  • Optional discovery service
  • Plugin runtime broker

docs.title: Single-Container Requirement
docs.text:
Version 1 must not require operators to deploy separate services for:

  • Database
  • Queue
  • Scheduler
  • Artifact generator
  • Transcoder coordinator
  • Web UI

Internal processes or workers may still exist inside the container.

docs.title: Process Model
docs.text:
The container may run:

  • One application process
  • Child FFmpeg processes
  • Optional isolated plugin processes
  • Internal worker threads

The container entrypoint must remain the parent supervisor for application lifecycle.

docs.title: Application Image
docs.text:
The official image must:

  • Contain the ChannelForge application
  • Contain or provide a supported FFmpeg build
  • Contain required runtime dependencies
  • Use a minimal supported base image
  • Declare application version metadata
  • Expose documented ports
  • Define a health check or documented external probe
  • Run as non-root where practical
  • Avoid unnecessary package managers and build tools in final image
  • Support amd64
  • Support arm64 when release validation permits
  • Include license and notice material
  • Produce a software bill of materials where practical

docs.title: Image Tags
docs.text:
Recommended tag classes:

  • Immutable release tag
  • Major-minor convenience tag
  • Stable channel
  • Beta channel
  • Development or edge channel
  • Digest reference

Examples:

channel-forge/channel-forge:1.0.0
channel-forge/channel-forge:1.0
channel-forge/channel-forge:stable
channel-forge/channel-forge:beta

Exact registry and naming remain implementation decisions.

docs.title: Immutable Deployments
docs.text:
Production deployments should prefer:

  • Exact version tag
  • Image digest
  • Recorded release notes

Floating tags simplify updates but reduce reproducibility.

docs.title: Image Metadata
docs.text:
The image should publish labels for:

  • Application name
  • Application version
  • Source repository
  • Revision
  • Build timestamp
  • License
  • Documentation
  • Vendor
  • Supported architecture

docs.title: Multi-Architecture Images
docs.text:
A multi-architecture manifest may include:

  • linux/amd64
  • linux/arm64

Architecture support requires:

  • Build success
  • Test success
  • FFmpeg compatibility
  • Native dependency compatibility
  • Hardware acceleration documentation

docs.title: Base Image
docs.text:
The base image should be:

  • Maintained
  • Minimal
  • Compatible with FFmpeg
  • Compatible with native SQLite dependencies
  • Compatible with supported hardware drivers
  • Scanned for vulnerabilities

docs.title: Image Build Stages
docs.text:
Recommended stages:

  1. Dependency resolution
  2. Application build
  3. Test or validation
  4. Runtime assembly
  5. Metadata and licenses

Build tools should not remain in the final image unless required.

docs.title: Reproducible Builds
docs.text:
The build should pin:

  • Dependency lockfile
  • Runtime version
  • Package manager version
  • Base image digest where feasible
  • FFmpeg source or package version
  • Native dependency versions

docs.title: FFmpeg Packaging
docs.text:
The image must make FFmpeg availability predictable.

Supported strategies:

  • Bundle a tested FFmpeg binary
  • Install from a pinned base repository
  • Use an official companion package during build

The application must report:

  • FFmpeg path
  • FFmpeg version
  • Enabled encoders
  • Enabled decoders
  • Enabled protocols
  • Hardware capabilities

docs.title: FFmpeg Override
docs.text:
Advanced deployments may provide an alternate FFmpeg binary.

An override must:

  • Be explicit
  • Be validated on startup
  • Report version
  • Report capabilities
  • Produce a warning when untested
  • Avoid arbitrary user-controlled command path changes through ordinary UI

docs.title: Container User
docs.text:
The container should run as a non-root user.

The runtime user requires:

  • Read and write access to ChannelForge data
  • Read and write access to temporary storage
  • Read access to mapped media paths when used
  • Access to configured hardware devices
  • Access to backup destination when used

docs.title: PUID and PGID
docs.text:
The image may support PUID and PGID compatibility for Unraid and common home server workflows.

Behavior must be documented.

Requirements:

  • Validate numeric values
  • Avoid silently running as root
  • Apply ownership only to managed paths
  • Avoid recursive ownership changes over large external media libraries
  • Report effective UID and GID at startup

docs.title: Supplemental Groups
docs.text:
Hardware and media access may require supplemental groups.

Examples:

  • video
  • render
  • Media-share group

Group IDs should be configurable without rebuilding the image.

docs.title: Root Execution
docs.text:
Running as root should:

  • Be unnecessary
  • Produce a warning
  • Be reserved for exceptional troubleshooting
  • Not disable application-level security
  • Not be required for standard hardware acceleration

docs.title: Filesystem Layout
docs.text:
Suggested in-container paths:

/config
/data
/cache
/tmp/channel-forge
/backups
/media

Exact paths may be consolidated.

The deployment contract must distinguish:

  • Durable configuration and database
  • Durable managed assets
  • Rebuildable cache
  • Temporary runtime files
  • Optional backup destination
  • Optional read-only media mounts

docs.title: Durable Data Root
docs.text:
One mounted durable root is preferred.

Example:

/config

It may contain:

/config/
  database/
  assets/
  artifacts/
  plugins/
  secrets/
  logs/
  backups/
  state/

Exact directory names are implementation details.

docs.title: Durable Data Requirements
docs.text:
Durable storage must preserve:

  • SQLite database
  • Managed files
  • Artwork
  • Branding
  • Presentation assets
  • Plugin packages
  • Plugin state
  • Output artifacts
  • Secret ciphertext
  • Audit
  • Migration metadata
  • Backup metadata

docs.title: Rebuildable Data
docs.text:
Rebuildable storage may include:

  • Search projections
  • Provider artwork cache
  • Temporary transcode cache
  • Temporary HLS segments
  • Generated diagnostics
  • Download staging
  • Upload staging

docs.title: Temporary Storage
docs.text:
Temporary storage must support:

  • FFmpeg pipes or intermediate files
  • HLS segments
  • Upload staging
  • Backup staging
  • Restore staging
  • Plugin temporary files
  • Artifact generation

docs.title: Temporary Storage Requirements
docs.text:
Temporary storage must:

  • Be writable
  • Have sufficient free space
  • Be cleaned on startup and shutdown
  • Be bounded
  • Be excluded from authoritative backup
