  • Avoid persistence requirements
  • Remain on a filesystem suitable for active workloads

docs.title: Memory-Backed Temporary Storage
docs.text:
A tmpfs may be used for small temporary workloads.

Risks:

  • Memory exhaustion
  • Segment loss on restart
  • Insufficient capacity for backups
  • OOM termination

ChannelForge must not require tmpfs.

docs.title: SQLite Storage Requirements
docs.text:
SQLite database storage must:

  • Be local or provide reliable POSIX-like locking semantics
  • Support atomic file replacement
  • Support WAL behavior where enabled
  • Avoid unsupported network filesystems
  • Have sufficient free space
  • Be writable by the container user
  • Be backed up through SQLite-aware workflow

docs.title: Unsupported SQLite Storage
docs.text:
The primary database should not be placed on:

  • Unreliable SMB mounts
  • Unreliable NFS configurations
  • Cloud-synchronized folders
  • Object-storage mounts
  • Filesystems lacking correct locking
  • Temporary container layers

Unless explicitly validated, these are unsupported.

docs.title: Unraid Appdata
docs.text:
On Unraid, durable state should use an appdata path such as:

/mnt/user/appdata/channelforge

A cache-pool-backed appdata location is preferred for SQLite performance.

The exact host path is operator-configurable.

docs.title: Unraid Share Considerations
docs.text:
Unraid documentation should address:

  • Cache pool
  • Mover behavior
  • SQLite locking
  • Share allocation
  • Backup location
  • Permissions
  • Case sensitivity
  • Direct disk paths versus user shares

docs.title: Media Mounts
docs.text:
Media mounts are optional because Plex, Jellyfin, and Emby can provide streams.

Local media mounts are used only when:

  • Path Mapping is configured
  • The provider reports usable paths
  • ChannelForge can read the same files
  • Local access is preferred by policy

docs.title: Read-Only Media Mounts
docs.text:
Media mounts should be read-only by default.

Example:

volumes:
  - /mnt/media:/media:ro

docs.title: Path Mapping
docs.text:
Host and container path differences must be configured explicitly.

Example:

Provider path: /movies
Container path: /media/movies

Windows provider paths may require a mapping such as:

Provider path: D:\Movies
Container path: /media/movies

docs.title: Mount Propagation
docs.text: ChannelForge should not require special mount propagation.

docs.title: Symlink Behavior
docs.text:
Media symlink handling must be documented.

The default should avoid escaping approved roots.

docs.title: File Permissions
docs.text:
The container startup check must verify:

  • Data root readable
  • Data root writable
  • Database directory writable
  • Managed asset directory writable
  • Temporary directory writable
  • Backup destination writable when configured
  • Media roots readable when configured

docs.title: Disk Capacity
docs.text:
ChannelForge should monitor free space for:

  • Data root
  • Temporary root
  • Backup root
  • HLS segment storage

docs.title: Disk Thresholds
docs.text:
Suggested states:

  • Healthy
  • Warning
  • Critical
  • Write-blocking

Exact thresholds are configurable.

docs.title: Disk Exhaustion Behavior
docs.text:
When disk is critically low:

  • Stop nonessential artifact generation
  • Stop large imports
  • Stop backup creation
  • Stop plugin cache growth
  • Preserve active publication
  • Serve prior valid artifacts
  • Raise critical health finding
  • Avoid repeated failing writes

docs.title: Configuration Sources
docs.text:
Configuration may come from:

  1. Environment variables
  2. Mounted secret files
  3. Command-line arguments
  4. Persisted instance configuration
  5. Safe built-in defaults

docs.title: Configuration Precedence
docs.text:
Precedence must be explicit and documented.

Recommended:

Command line
Environment or secret file
Persisted instance configuration
Built-in default

Some bootstrap values must remain deployment-controlled and not editable in the database.

docs.title: Bootstrap Configuration
docs.text:
Bootstrap configuration may include:

  • Data path
  • HTTP bind address
  • HTTP port
  • Public base URL bootstrap
  • Database path
  • Temporary path
  • Secret key reference
  • Log level
  • Trusted proxy bootstrap
  • Deployment mode

docs.title: Persisted Configuration
docs.text:
Persisted settings may include:

  • Networks
  • Channels
  • Media Sources
  • Schedule policy
  • Output profiles
  • Backup policy
  • Retention
  • Public artifact policy
  • Plugin policy

docs.title: Environment Variable Naming
docs.text:
Environment variables should use a consistent prefix.

Example:

CHANNELFORGE_

docs.title: Environment Variable Rules
docs.text:
Environment variables must:

  • Have documented type
  • Have documented default
  • Fail clearly on invalid values
  • Avoid silent coercion
  • Avoid containing reusable secrets where a secret file is supported
  • Be listed in diagnostics without secret values

docs.title: Example Bootstrap Variables
docs.text:
Potential variables:

CHANNELFORGE_DATA_DIR
CHANNELFORGE_TEMP_DIR
CHANNELFORGE_HTTP_HOST
CHANNELFORGE_HTTP_PORT
CHANNELFORGE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL
CHANNELFORGE_LOG_LEVEL
CHANNELFORGE_TIME_ZONE
CHANNELFORGE_TRUSTED_PROXIES
CHANNELFORGE_SECRET_KEY_FILE
CHANNELFORGE_PUID
CHANNELFORGE_PGID

Exact names remain implementation details.

docs.title: Time Zone
docs.text:
The container should normally use UTC internally.

Instance and Channel editorial time zones are stored explicitly.

A deployment time-zone variable may affect:

  • Log display
  • Backup naming
  • Operator-facing defaults

It must not replace Channel IANA time-zone configuration.

docs.title: System Clock
docs.text:
The container uses the host clock.

The deployment must provide accurate time.

docs.title: Clock Requirements
docs.text:
The host should use reliable time synchronization.

ChannelForge should report:

  • Current UTC time
  • Detected clock anomalies
  • Token validation issues
  • Schedule drift risk

docs.title: Locale
docs.text:
The runtime should not depend on host locale for:

  • Timestamp parsing
  • Number parsing
  • Duration parsing
  • Schedule sorting
  • Database ordering

docs.title: Secrets Deployment
docs.text:
Secret values should be supplied through:

  • Mounted secret files
  • Container secrets where available
  • Environment variables only when necessary
  • Initial UI entry stored through encrypted Secret Service

docs.title: Master Key
docs.text:
The secret-encryption master key must be external to the encrypted database values.

Recommended deployment options:

  • Mounted read-only secret file
  • Docker secret
  • Unraid file with restrictive permissions
  • Host keyring integration in future

docs.title: Master Key File
docs.text:
The key file should:

  • Be readable only by application user
  • Be mounted read-only
  • Not be stored inside public appdata backup unless intentionally protected
  • Be included in disaster-recovery planning
  • Be excluded from logs and support bundles

docs.title: Missing Master Key
docs.text:
Startup behavior must be explicit.

Possible behavior:

  • Fail readiness
  • Enter recovery mode
  • Permit limited read-only access
  • Require key restoration
  • Avoid regenerating a new key silently

Silently replacing a missing key is prohibited.

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text: A supported Compose example must be maintained with releases.

docs.title: Compose Requirements
docs.text:
The Compose definition should include:

  • Image
  • Container name
  • Restart policy
  • Port mappings
  • Durable volume
  • Temporary volume
  • Optional backup volume
  • Environment
  • Secret file
  • Health check
  • Optional device mappings
  • Optional supplemental groups
  • Optional reverse-proxy labels separated from core example

docs.title: Reference Compose Structure
docs.text:
services:
  channelforge:
    image: channel-forge/channel-forge:1.0.0
    container_name: channelforge
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    volumes:
      - ./config:/config
      - ./tmp:/tmp/channel-forge
      - ./secrets/master-key:/run/secrets/channel-forge-master-key:ro
    environment:
      CHANNELFORGE_DATA_DIR: /config
      CHANNELFORGE_TEMP_DIR: /tmp/channel-forge
      CHANNELFORGE_HTTP_PORT: "8000"
      CHANNELFORGE_SECRET_KEY_FILE: /run/secrets/channel-forge-master-key
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "channel-forge-healthcheck"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 60s

This is conceptual and not a final release file.

docs.title: Compose Version
docs.text: Use current Compose specification syntax rather than depending on obsolete version keys.

docs.title: Restart Policy
docs.text:
Recommended default:

unless-stopped

Alternative:

on-failure

The operator should understand that automatic restart does not repair:

  • Corrupt database
  • Missing key
  • Invalid migration
  • Permission failure
  • Disk full

docs.title: Compose Profiles
docs.text:
Optional profiles may separate examples for:

  • NVIDIA
  • Intel or VA-API
  • Reverse proxy
  • Host networking
  • Development
  • Backup testing

docs.title: Compose Networks
docs.text:
A dedicated bridge network is recommended.

Media servers may be reachable through:

  • Same Docker network
  • Host LAN address
  • DNS name
  • Reverse-proxy address

docs.title: Container DNS
docs.text: The deployment must provide DNS resolution for configured Media Sources.

docs.title: host.docker.internal
docs.text:
This hostname is platform-dependent.

Documentation should not assume it exists on every Linux host.

docs.title: Linux Host Gateway
docs.text: Compose may support a host-gateway mapping when the operator needs to reach a host service.

docs.title: Port Mapping
docs.text:
The application HTTP port is configurable.

Example:

8000/tcp

docs.title: Port Collision
docs.text:
The operator may map any unused host port to the container port.

Public artifact and stream URLs must use the configured external address.

docs.title: Separate Ports
docs.text:
Version 1 should prefer one HTTP port for:

  • UI
  • Management API
  • Streams
  • XMLTV
  • M3U
  • HDHomeRun-compatible HTTP endpoints

A separate discovery UDP port may be required.

docs.title: UDP Discovery
docs.text: HDHomeRun-compatible discovery may require UDP broadcast or multicast behavior.

docs.title: Discovery Deployment Modes
docs.text:
Possible modes:

  • Disabled
  • Bridged network with explicit UDP mapping
  • Host network
  • Macvlan or ipvlan
  • External discovery relay

docs.title: Host Networking
docs.text:
Host networking may simplify discovery.

Risks:

  • Broader port exposure
  • Reduced network isolation
  • Port conflicts
  • Harder firewall assumptions
  • Platform differences

It should not be required for normal M3U or XMLTV use.

docs.title: Discovery Interface Selection
docs.text:
The operator should be able to select:

  • One interface
  • One address
  • One subnet
  • All interfaces under warning

docs.title: Static Tuner Configuration
docs.text:
Clients that allow manual tuner URL entry do not require broadcast discovery.

Documentation should prefer manual configuration when it avoids host networking.

docs.title: Docker Desktop
docs.text:
Docker Desktop may be useful for development and testing.

It is not the primary recommended production environment.

Potential differences:

  • Host networking
  • UDP broadcast
  • Filesystem performance
  • Device passthrough
  • Path mappings
  • Clock behavior
  • Sleep and resume

docs.title: Windows Host Development
docs.text:
On Windows:

  • Store the repository on a local filesystem
  • Use Linux containers
  • Expect path conversion
  • Do not rely on Windows paths inside the container
  • Use explicit media Path Mappings
  • Expect limited hardware and discovery differences

docs.title: Unraid Deployment
docs.text: ChannelForge should provide an Unraid-compatible template.

docs.title: Unraid Template Fields
docs.text:
Required fields may include:

  • Name
  • Repository
  • Network type
  • Web UI URL
  • Icon
  • Support URL
  • Project URL
  • Config path
  • Temporary path
  • Backup path
  • HTTP port
  • Discovery port
  • PUID
  • PGID
  • Time zone
  • Master key path
  • Public base URL
  • Log level
  • Optional GPU devices

docs.title: Unraid Template Defaults
docs.text:
Defaults should:

  • Avoid root
  • Use appdata
  • Avoid public exposure
  • Disable discovery unless configured
  • Use bridge networking unless host networking is required
  • Avoid mounting the whole host filesystem
  • Avoid write access to media
  • Provide clear descriptions

docs.title: Unraid Web UI Link
docs.text:
The template should produce a Web UI link based on:

  • Host address
  • Mapped HTTP port
  • Base path if configured

docs.title: Unraid Network Types
docs.text:
Supported examples:

  • Bridge
  • Host
  • Custom Docker network
  • Custom IP

Each has different discovery behavior.

docs.title: Unraid Custom IP
docs.text:
A custom IP may improve:

  • Stable tuner address
  • Discovery
  • Port isolation

It may complicate:

  • Host access
  • Routing
  • macvlan stability
  • Firewall behavior

docs.title: Unraid Host Access
docs.text: When using custom networks, Media Sources running on the Unraid host must remain reachable.

docs.title: Unraid GPU Mapping
docs.text:
The template may support:

  • /dev/dri
  • NVIDIA runtime variables
  • Other device paths when validated

docs.title: Unraid Appdata Backup
docs.text:
Documentation should integrate with common appdata backup practices while clarifying that:

  • SQLite-aware backup is preferred
  • Copying a live database directory may be inconsistent
  • ChannelForge's internal backup should be used for authoritative recovery
  • External appdata backup should stop the container or use a verified snapshot

docs.title: Reverse Proxy
docs.text: ChannelForge may run behind a reverse proxy.

docs.title: Reverse Proxy Responsibilities
docs.text:
A proxy may provide:

  • TLS
  • Public hostname
  • Authentication
  • Access logging
  • Compression
  • IP allowlisting
  • Rate limiting
  • Request size control

docs.title: Reverse Proxy Requirements
docs.text:
The proxy must support:

  • Long-lived streaming responses
  • Disabled response buffering for streams
  • Suitable read timeouts
  • WebSocket only if future features require it
  • Server-Sent Events if enabled
  • Large artifact downloads
  • Correct forwarded headers
  • No caching of authenticated management responses

docs.title: Trusted Proxy Configuration
docs.text: ChannelForge trusts forwarded headers only from configured proxy addresses.

docs.title: Forwarded Headers
docs.text:
Potential headers:

  • Forwarded
  • X-Forwarded-For
  • X-Forwarded-Proto
  • X-Forwarded-Host

The exact trusted set must be documented.

docs.title: Public Base URL
docs.text:
A reverse-proxied deployment should set an explicit public base URL.

Example:

https://tv.example.net

This affects:

  • M3U stream URLs
  • XMLTV links
  • HDHomeRun lineup URLs
  • Logo URLs
  • API links
  • Download links

docs.title: Base Path
docs.text:
A proxy may host ChannelForge under a base path.

Example:

https://example.net/channelforge

Base-path support must be tested across:

  • UI
  • API
  • Static assets
  • Streams
  • HLS
  • XMLTV
  • M3U
  • HDHomeRun-compatible endpoints

Version 1 may declare root-path deployment as the supported default.

docs.title: Proxy Buffering
docs.text:
Proxy buffering must be disabled for:

  • MPEG-TS live streams
  • HLS segment generation paths where inappropriate
  • Server-Sent Events
  • Large streaming exports

docs.title: Proxy Timeouts
docs.text:
Timeouts must exceed expected:

  • Live stream duration
  • HLS connection behavior
  • Backup download
  • Large XMLTV download
  • Background Job polling

docs.title: Proxy Compression
docs.text:
Compression is appropriate for:

  • JSON
  • XMLTV
  • M3U
  • HTML
  • JavaScript
  • CSS

Compression is unnecessary for:

  • Video
  • Audio
  • Already-compressed images
  • Transport streams

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
TLS may terminate at the reverse proxy.

Direct ChannelForge TLS is optional unless implemented.

docs.title: HTTPS Recommendation
docs.text: Remote management access should use HTTPS.

docs.title: Local HTTP
docs.text:
Local HTTP may be acceptable on isolated trusted networks.

The UI must warn when secure cookie or token assumptions are weakened.

docs.title: Certificate Renewal
docs.text: Certificate renewal is the proxy or deployment operator's responsibility unless ChannelForge later manages TLS directly.

docs.title: HSTS
docs.text: Enable HSTS only when the hostname is permanently HTTPS.

docs.title: Authentication Proxy
docs.text:
Reverse-proxy authentication is optional.

It requires:

  • Trusted proxy addresses
  • Header stripping
  • Direct-access policy
  • User mapping
  • Documentation
  • Audit

docs.title: Network Exposure
docs.text:
The operator must be able to bind:

  • Loopback only
  • One LAN address
  • All addresses

docs.title: Default Bind
docs.text:
A container typically binds internally to all interfaces.

Host exposure is controlled through Docker port publishing.

docs.title: Public Internet Exposure
docs.text:
Direct public exposure is not recommended without:

  • TLS
  • Authentication
  • Secure proxy
  • Firewall
  • Updated release
  • Strong administrator password
  • Backup
  • Stream access policy
  • Plugin review

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
Document required ports:

  • HTTP TCP
  • Optional discovery UDP
  • Outbound connections to Media Sources
  • Outbound plugin destinations
  • Optional backup destination

docs.title: Outbound Networking
docs.text: ChannelForge requires outbound or lateral access to configured integrations.

docs.title: Media Source Connectivity
docs.text:
The container must reach:

  • Plex server address
  • Jellyfin server address
  • Emby server address

docs.title: DNS Names
docs.text: Use stable DNS names where possible.

docs.title: Address Changes
docs.text: A Media Source's stable provider identity protects against silent server replacement when an address changes.

docs.title: IPv6
docs.text:
Deployment must document whether:

  • HTTP binds IPv6
  • Discovery uses IPv6
  • Media Sources resolve IPv6
  • Firewall protects IPv6

docs.title: Air-Gapped Deployment
docs.text:
ChannelForge should remain usable without internet access when:

  • Container image is present
  • Plex, Jellyfin, or Emby are reachable
  • Plugin packages are local
  • No external metadata provider is required
  • Updates are performed manually

docs.title: Air-Gapped Limitations
docs.text:
Potential limitations:

  • No online update check
  • No remote plugin marketplace
  • No external metadata lookup
  • No vulnerability feed
  • No remote artwork provider

docs.title: Proxy Environment Variables
docs.text:
System-wide HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY may affect outbound integrations.

Support must be explicit.

docs.title: NO_PROXY
docs.text: Local Media Source addresses may require NO_PROXY.

docs.title: Source-Specific Proxy
docs.text: A source-specific proxy is preferable when only one integration requires it.

docs.title: Hardware Acceleration
docs.text: Hardware acceleration is optional.

docs.title: Hardware Support Categories
docs.text:
Potential categories:

  • Intel Quick Sync
  • VA-API
  • NVIDIA NVENC and NVDEC
  • AMD VA-API
  • VideoToolbox in nonprimary environments
  • Software fallback

docs.title: Hardware Detection
docs.text:
Startup should report:

  • Visible devices
  • Device permissions
  • FFmpeg hardware methods
  • Encoders
  • Decoders
  • Test status
  • Configured limits

docs.title: Hardware Preflight
docs.text:
A preflight may:

  • Open device
  • Query capabilities
  • Run a short synthetic transcode
  • Verify output
  • Release device

docs.title: Intel and VA-API
docs.text:
Typical Linux access uses:

/dev/dri

The container user may need membership in:

  • video
  • render

docs.title: Device Mapping
docs.text:
Example:

devices:
  - /dev/dri:/dev/dri

docs.title: NVIDIA
docs.text:
NVIDIA deployment may require:

  • Compatible host driver
  • NVIDIA Container Toolkit
  • Runtime configuration
  • Device selection
  • Driver capabilities
  • FFmpeg build with NVIDIA support

docs.title: NVIDIA Environment
docs.text:
The exact environment variable pattern depends on the container runtime.

It must be documented in a separate validated example.

docs.title: AMD
docs.text:
AMD acceleration may use VA-API through /dev/dri.

Support depends on:

  • Host driver
  • Device generation
  • FFmpeg build
  • Codec
  • Container permissions

docs.title: Hardware Device Isolation
docs.text: Expose only required devices.

docs.title: Hardware Concurrency
docs.text: ChannelForge must enforce configured concurrent hardware sessions.

docs.title: Hardware Failure
docs.text:
Hardware failure may:

  • Fall back to software
  • Fall back to another device
  • Reduce output profile
  • Fail the session

Deployment health should show hardware degradation.

docs.title: Software Transcoding
docs.text: Software transcoding requires sufficient CPU.

docs.title: CPU Sizing
docs.text:
Capacity depends on:

  • Codec
  • Resolution
  • Frame rate
  • Bit rate
  • Filters
  • Subtitle burn-in
  • Number of Channels
  • Client profile
  • Source format

No universal CPU minimum guarantees real-time transcoding.

docs.title: Resource Profiles
docs.text:
Documentation may define qualitative profiles:

  • Metadata and direct-stream only
  • One HD transcode
  • Multiple HD transcodes
  • 4K transcode
  • Always-on multi-Channel

These require benchmark validation.

docs.title: CPU Limits
docs.text:
Container CPU limits are optional.

Limits that are too low may cause:

  • Stream stalls
  • FFmpeg slowdown
  • Schedule transition delay
  • Background Job delay

docs.title: CPU Shares
docs.text: Background work should yield to active playout.

docs.title: Memory Sizing
docs.text:
Memory use includes:

  • Application runtime
  • SQLite cache
  • Catalog projections
  • Schedule generation
  • FFmpeg
  • HLS buffers
  • Plugin processes
  • Uploads
  • Backup staging

docs.title: Memory Limits
docs.text: A hard memory limit should allow peak workload.

docs.title: OOM Behavior
docs.text:
On out-of-memory termination:

  • Container may restart
  • Running sessions become abandoned
  • SQLite transactions roll back
  • Startup reconciliation runs
  • HLS segments are rebuilt
  • Health records the abnormal termination when detectable

docs.title: Swap
docs.text: Heavy swap can break real-time playout.

docs.title: Process Limits
docs.text:
The deployment may limit:

  • PIDs
  • Open files
  • Threads
  • Child processes

Limits must accommodate FFmpeg and plugins.

docs.title: File Descriptor Limits
docs.text: Live clients and provider connections consume file descriptors.

docs.title: Network Bandwidth
docs.text:
Required bandwidth includes:

  • Media Source input
  • Client output
  • Multiple simultaneous clients
  • Artwork synchronization
  • Backups
  • HLS overhead

docs.title: Shared Streams
docs.text: Shared Channel Sessions reduce duplicate input and transcode cost.

docs.title: Quality Profiles
docs.text: Output profiles should be chosen according to host capacity.

docs.title: Resource Admission
docs.text: ChannelForge should reject or queue work rather than exceed configured limits.

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text: Health checks are required for orchestration and operator diagnostics.

docs.title: Liveness
docs.text:
Liveness answers whether the application process can respond.

Suggested path:

/health/live

Liveness should not depend on:

  • Media Sources
  • FFmpeg
  • Backup destination
  • Plugins
  • External internet

docs.title: Readiness
docs.text:
Readiness answers whether normal service can be accepted.

Suggested path:

/health/ready

Readiness may depend on:

  • Startup complete
  • Database open
  • Migrations complete
  • Data root writable
  • Secret key available
  • Critical reconciliation complete
  • Not in restore activation
  • HTTP service initialized

docs.title: Detailed Health
docs.text:
Authenticated detailed health may include:

  • Persistence
  • Disk
  • FFmpeg
  • Hardware
  • Media Sources
  • Plugins
  • Output artifacts
  • Background Jobs
  • Backup freshness
  • Clock
  • Version

docs.title: Container Health Check
docs.text:
The image should include a small health-check command or HTTP client.

It must:

  • Avoid requiring curl if not otherwise needed
  • Have a short timeout
  • Return nonzero on failure
  • Use localhost
  • Avoid authentication for liveness
  • Avoid leaking details

docs.title: Start Period
docs.text:
The health check should allow time for:

  • Database migration
  • Integrity checks
  • Large reconciliation
  • Plugin initialization

docs.title: Readiness During Migration
docs.text: Readiness remains false until migration succeeds.

docs.title: Health During Maintenance
docs.text:
Liveness may remain true.

Readiness may be false or degraded depending on maintenance type.

docs.title: Startup Sequence
docs.text:
Recommended startup sequence:

  1. Initialize process logging.
  2. Report build and runtime version.
  3. Validate effective user.
  4. Validate data and temp paths.
  5. Load bootstrap configuration.
  6. Load master key.
  7. Open SQLite.
  8. Apply connection settings.
  9. Verify schema.
  10. Create pre-migration backup when required.
  11. Apply migrations.
  12. Run quick integrity check.
  13. Reconcile managed files.
  14. Reconcile abandoned jobs.
  15. Reconcile playout sessions.
  16. Validate FFmpeg.
  17. Detect hardware.
  18. Load plugin registrations.
  19. Start enabled plugins.
  20. Validate active publications.
  21. Validate active artifacts.
  22. Start Background Job workers.
  23. Start HTTP readiness.
  24. Start optional discovery.
  25. Mark ready.

docs.title: Startup Logs
docs.text:
Startup logs should clearly report:

  • Application version
  • Build revision
  • Database schema version
  • Data path
  • Effective UID and GID
  • HTTP bind
  • Public base URL
  • FFmpeg version
  • Hardware status
  • Plugin count
  • Migration result
  • Readiness result

Secrets must be redacted.

docs.title: Startup Failure
docs.text:
A blocking startup failure must:

  • Exit nonzero or remain explicitly unready
  • Log an actionable reason
  • Avoid infinite rapid restart loops where possible
  • Preserve data
  • Avoid partial migration continuation
  • Avoid silently resetting configuration

docs.title: Recovery Mode
docs.text:
Certain failures may start a restricted recovery mode.

Examples:

  • Missing encryption key
  • Restore required
  • Plugin framework failure
  • Noncritical artifact corruption

Recovery mode must not expose normal privileged operations without authentication.

docs.title: Shutdown Signal
docs.text: The container must handle normal stop signals.

docs.title: Graceful Shutdown
docs.text:
Recommended shutdown sequence:

  1. Mark unready.
  2. Stop accepting new management mutations.
  3. Stop accepting new stream sessions where policy permits.
  4. Request Background Job cancellation.
  5. Drain bounded plugin calls.
  6. Stop discovery.
  7. Stop or finalize playout sessions.
  8. Terminate FFmpeg processes.
  9. Finalize Airing Records.
  10. Flush audit and Outbox.
  11. Checkpoint SQLite where appropriate.
  12. Close database.
  13. Remove temporary leases.
  14. Exit.

docs.title: Shutdown Timeout
docs.text: Docker stop timeout should exceed the normal graceful shutdown budget.

docs.title: Forced Shutdown
docs.text:
If the process is force-killed:

  • SQLite should recover committed transactions
  • Startup reconciliation handles abandoned jobs and sessions
  • Temporary files are cleaned
  • Hardware reservations expire
  • Previous valid artifacts remain

docs.title: Restart Behavior
docs.text:
Container restart must not:

  • Create a new instance identity
  • Delete schedules
  • Delete credentials
  • Reset plugins
  • Reset channel numbers
  • Regenerate master key
  • Change public URLs silently

docs.title: Restart Policy and Crash Loop
docs.text:
Repeated startup failure should be visible.

Documentation should show how to inspect:

  • Container logs
  • Health state
  • Data permissions
  • Master key
  • Migration error
  • Disk capacity

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text: Database migrations run at startup or through a controlled command.

docs.title: Migration Requirements
docs.text:
• Ordered
  • Checksum verified
  • Exclusive
  • Backed up
  • Logged
  • Fail closed
  • Restart-safe where possible

docs.title: Pre-Migration Backup
docs.text:
A pre-migration backup should be created when:

  • Schema changes are destructive
  • Secret format changes
  • Plugin framework changes
  • Release policy requires it

docs.title: Migration Storage Headroom
docs.text: Migrations may require temporary disk equal to a substantial fraction of database size.

docs.title: Migration Failure
docs.text:
On failure:

  • Do not mark ready
  • Preserve pre-migration backup
  • Preserve database
  • Exit or remain in recovery
  • Provide migration ID
  • Avoid automatic downgrade

docs.title: Large Migration
docs.text:
Large data backfills may:

  • Run before readiness
  • Run in resumable maintenance mode
  • Run after startup under compatibility behavior

The release notes must state the impact.

docs.title: Upgrade Policy
docs.text: An upgrade replaces the container image while retaining durable storage.

docs.title: Upgrade Workflow
docs.text:
Recommended:

  1. Read release notes.
  2. Verify current backup.
  3. Create fresh backup.
  4. Record current image tag or digest.
  5. Pull target image.
  6. Stop ChannelForge.
  7. Start target image with same storage.
  8. Monitor migration.
  9. Verify readiness.
  10. Verify Media Sources.
  11. Verify XMLTV and M3U.
  12. Verify one Channel stream.
  13. Retain prior image until confidence established.

docs.title: Automatic Updates
docs.text:
Unattended automatic updates are not recommended by default.

Reasons:

  • Schema migration
  • Plugin compatibility
  • FFmpeg changes
  • Hardware regressions
  • Output compatibility
  • Security-setting changes

docs.title: Update Notification
docs.text:
ChannelForge may report that a newer version exists.

It should not automatically install without explicit policy.

docs.title: Release Channels
docs.text:
Potential channels:

  • Stable
  • Beta
  • Edge

docs.title: Stable Channel
docs.text:
Stable releases require:

  • Migration testing
  • Compose testing
  • Unraid testing
  • Plex, Jellyfin, and Emby compatibility checks
  • Stream compatibility checks
  • Backup and restore test
  • Security review
  • Release notes

docs.title: Beta Channel
docs.text:
Beta releases may contain:

  • New architecture
  • Incomplete migrations
  • Compatibility warnings
  • Higher diagnostic verbosity

They should not be recommended for critical always-on deployments without backup.

docs.title: Edge Channel
docs.text:
Edge builds are development artifacts.

They may be unsupported for migration continuity.

docs.title: Downgrade
docs.text: Downgrade is not guaranteed.

docs.title: Downgrade Restrictions
docs.text: A prior image must not start against a newer incompatible schema.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: Rollback means returning to a prior application and compatible data state.

docs.title: Safe Rollback
docs.text:
Possible when:

  • No incompatible migration occurred
  • Prior image supports current schema
  • No irreversible secret migration occurred
  • Plugins remain compatible

docs.title: Backup-Based Rollback
docs.text:
When schema changed incompatibly:

  1. Stop current container.
  2. Preserve failed current data.
  3. Restore pre-upgrade backup.
  4. Start prior image.
  5. Verify.
  6. Investigate before retry.

docs.title: Rollback Documentation
docs.text:
Every release with migration must document:

  • Whether direct rollback is supported
  • Whether backup restore is required
  • Plugin implications
  • Secret key implications
  • Artifact implications

docs.title: Backup Deployment
docs.text: ChannelForge's internal backup workflow is authoritative.

docs.title: Backup Destination
docs.text:
Version 1 may support:

  • Path inside durable storage
  • Separate mounted local path
  • Mounted network backup destination
  • User download

docs.title: Separate Backup Mount
docs.text:
A separate backup mount is recommended.

Example:

/backups

docs.title: Backup Permissions
docs.text: The container user needs write access only to the intended backup path.

docs.title: Backup Scheduling
docs.text: Backup scheduling is application configuration.

docs.title: Host-Level Backup
docs.text:
Host-level backup may supplement internal backups.

It should:

  • Stop the container, or
  • Use a filesystem snapshot with SQLite consistency, or
  • Copy a verified internal backup archive

docs.title: Appdata Copy Warning
docs.text: Copying live SQLite files without WAL awareness is not a guaranteed backup.

docs.title: Restore Deployment
docs.text:
Restore may be performed through:

  • Authenticated UI
  • Controlled CLI
  • Recovery-mode command
  • Replacement container against staged data

docs.title: Restore Staging
docs.text:
Restore requires sufficient storage for:

  • Current data
  • Backup archive
  • Extracted staging data
  • Safety backup

docs.title: Restore and Container Identity
docs.text: Restoring data should preserve instance identity unless cross-instance restore policy changes it.

docs.title: Disaster Recovery
docs.text:
Required recovery materials:

  • Backup archive
  • Master key or backup passphrase
  • Container image or version
  • Deployment configuration
  • Volume paths
  • Plugin packages where not embedded
  • Documentation

docs.title: Disaster Recovery Drill
docs.text:
Operators should periodically verify:

  • Backup download
  • Backup checksum
  • Key availability
  • Test restore
  • Application startup
  • Schedule visibility
  • Stream playback

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Container logs go to standard output and standard error.

docs.title: Log Format
docs.text:
Support:

  • Human-readable
  • Structured JSON

docs.title: Log Level
docs.text:
Suggested levels:

  • Error
  • Warn
  • Info
  • Debug
  • Trace

docs.title: Default Log Level
docs.text: Default should be INFO.

docs.title: Debug Logging
docs.text:
Debug mode:

  • Is temporary
  • Preserves redaction
  • May increase disk and CPU use
  • Should not be left enabled indefinitely

docs.title: Docker Logging Driver
docs.text: The operator is responsible for log-driver configuration.

docs.title: Log Rotation
docs.text:
Unbounded Docker JSON logs can consume the host disk.

Documentation must recommend rotation.

docs.title: Managed File Logs
docs.text:
ChannelForge may optionally store bounded operational logs in managed storage.

They must not replace standard container logs.

docs.title: Access Logs
docs.text:
HTTP access logging should:

  • Use route templates
  • Redact query tokens
  • Omit Authorization
  • Bound client-address retention
  • Distinguish stream requests

docs.title: FFmpeg Logs
docs.text:
FFmpeg logs are:

  • Bounded
  • Session-associated
  • Redacted
  • Exposed only to authorized diagnostics

docs.title: Plugin Logs
docs.text:
Plugin logs are:

  • Namespaced
  • Rate-limited
  • Redacted
  • Bounded

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
Version 1 should provide:

  • Health endpoints
  • Structured logs
  • Internal metrics
  • Background Job status
  • Runtime status
  • Diagnostic bundles

docs.title: Metrics Endpoint
docs.text:
A metrics endpoint may be:

  • Disabled by default
  • Authenticated
  • Bound to local interface
  • Prometheus compatible

docs.title: Metrics Security
docs.text:
Metrics may reveal:

  • Channel names
  • Source health
  • Runtime capacity
  • Host details

Exposure must be controlled.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.text:
Distributed tracing is optional for version 1.

Local correlation IDs remain required.

docs.title: Support Bundle
docs.text: An operator may generate a support bundle.

docs.title: Support Bundle Contents
docs.text:
Potential contents:

  • Application version
  • Build revision
  • Effective nonsecret configuration
  • Schema version
  • Migration status
  • Health summary
  • FFmpeg version and capabilities
  • Hardware summary
  • Plugin manifests
  • Recent redacted logs
  • Job summaries
  • Database integrity result
  • Storage capacity
  • Network endpoint classification
  • Compose or template diagnostics supplied by operator

docs.title: Support Bundle Exclusions
docs.text:
Exclude:

  • Passwords
  • API tokens
  • Session tokens
  • Provider tokens
  • Plugin secrets
  • Master key
  • Backup passphrases
  • Signed source URLs
  • Raw cookies
  • Private keys

docs.title: Support Bundle Size
docs.text:
The bundle is bounded.

Large logs are truncated or sampled.

docs.title: Support Bundle Audit
docs.text: Generating and downloading a bundle is audited.

docs.title: Diagnostic Command
docs.text:
The image may include a CLI diagnostic command.

Potential actions:

  • Print version
  • Validate paths
  • Test database
  • Test FFmpeg
  • List hardware
  • Test Media Source reachability
  • Verify backup
  • Generate support bundle

docs.title: CLI Security
docs.text: CLI commands should not print secrets.

docs.title: Deployment Validation
docs.text:
A deployment validation command may check:

  • Effective UID
  • Writable data root
  • Writable temp root
  • Master key
  • SQLite locking
  • FFmpeg
  • HTTP port
  • Public base URL
  • Device access
  • Backup path
  • DNS
  • Trusted proxy configuration

docs.title: Monitoring Recommendations
docs.text:
Operators should monitor:

  • Container health
  • Restart count
  • Disk free space
  • Database size
  • WAL size
  • Backup age
  • Active sessions
  • Transcode capacity
  • Source health
  • Artifact freshness
  • Job failures

docs.title: Alert Recommendations
docs.text:
Potential alerts:

  • Container unhealthy
  • Repeated restart
  • Disk critical
  • Backup stale
  • Database integrity failure
  • Migration failure
  • FFmpeg unavailable
  • Hardware unavailable
  • No active publication
  • XMLTV stale
  • Plugin quarantined

docs.title: Security Hardening
docs.text:
Recommended Docker security options:

  • Non-root user
  • No privileged mode
  • Drop unnecessary capabilities
  • No Docker socket
  • Read-only root filesystem where compatible
  • No-new-privileges
  • Restrictive seccomp
  • Device allowlist
  • Bounded resources
  • Restricted published ports
  • Read-only media mounts
  • Secret files
  • Updated image

docs.title: Linux Capabilities
docs.text: ChannelForge should not require broad Linux capabilities.

docs.title: no-new-privileges
docs.text:
The deployment should support:

no-new-privileges

when hardware and runtime behavior permit.

docs.title: Read-Only Root Filesystem
docs.text:
A read-only root filesystem may be supported when writable paths are mounted for:

  • Data
  • Temp
  • Runtime process state

docs.title: Seccomp
docs.text:
Default Docker seccomp should remain enabled.

Custom profiles may be considered after validation.

docs.title: AppArmor and SELinux
docs.text: ChannelForge should work with standard confinement where volume labels and device permissions are configured correctly.

docs.title: Privileged Mode
docs.text: Privileged mode is prohibited for normal deployment.

docs.title: Docker Socket
docs.text:
Do not mount:

/var/run/docker.sock

docs.title: Host Filesystem
docs.text: Do not mount / or broad host paths.

docs.title: Secrets in Compose
docs.text: Avoid committing secrets directly in Compose YAML.

docs.title: File Ownership Changes
docs.text: Startup must not recursively chown large media trees.

docs.title: Release Artifacts
docs.text:

  • Migration notes

  • Rollback notes

docs.title: Unraid Template Release
docs.text: Template changes should be versioned and reviewed.

docs.title: Deployment Modes
docs.text:

docs.title: Mode Selection
docs.text:
Mode is deployment-controlled.

The UI cannot silently switch production into development mode.

docs.text:

The key must not be generated through weak shell randomness.

docs.text:

docs.title: Property Tests
docs.text:
Useful properties:

  • Recreating the container with the same durable volume preserves the instance.
  • Recreating the container without the durable volume creates a distinct empty installation.
  • Missing master key never causes silent key regeneration.
  • A failed migration never marks the instance ready.
  • A failed upgrade preserves the pre-upgrade backup.
  • A container restart does not modify approved Schedule Plans.
  • A read-only media mount is sufficient for local playback.
  • Temporary storage loss does not remove durable schedule state.
  • Public access remains disabled unless explicitly enabled.
  • Untrusted forwarded headers do not change authenticated identity.
  • Provider credentials do not appear in support bundles.
  • The image does not require privileged mode.
  • The image does not require Docker socket access.
  • Last valid XMLTV and M3U survive container recreation.
  • Restore activates only verified data.

docs.title: Reference Compose Deployment
docs.text:
Assume:

  • Linux host
  • ChannelForge data at /srv/channelforge
  • Temporary data at /srv/channelforge-tmp
  • Master key at /srv/secrets/channelforge-master-key
  • HTTP host port 8000
  • Jellyfin at http://192.168.0.15:8096

Expected behavior:

  • ChannelForge starts as non-root.
  • SQLite and managed files remain under durable storage.
  • Temporary files use the temporary mount.
  • The key is read from the secret mount.
  • Jellyfin is configured through the Web UI.
  • Container recreation preserves the instance.
  • Removing only the container does not remove schedules.
  • Removing the durable volume does remove the instance state.

docs.title: Reference Unraid Deployment
docs.text:
Assume:

  • Appdata path /mnt/user/appdata/channelforge
  • Backup path /mnt/user/backups/channelforge
  • Bridge networking
  • HTTP host port 8000
  • Jellyfin at a LAN address
  • Intel GPU exposed through /dev/dri

Expected behavior:

  • Appdata stores SQLite and managed files.
  • Backup archives use the backup path.
  • ChannelForge reaches Jellyfin through the LAN.
  • Hardware preflight identifies Intel acceleration.
  • Discovery remains disabled until explicitly configured.
  • The Unraid Web UI link opens ChannelForge.
  • Updating the image preserves appdata.

docs.title: Reference Reverse Proxy Deployment
docs.text:
Assume:

  • Public URL https://tv.example.net
  • Proxy terminates TLS
  • ChannelForge remains on an internal Docker network
  • Proxy buffering is disabled for streams
  • Trusted proxy address is configured

Expected behavior:

  • Generated M3U URLs use the public URL.
  • Secure cookies are used.
  • Forwarded scheme is accepted only from the trusted proxy.
  • Direct spoofed forwarding headers are ignored.
  • Live streams remain connected.
  • XMLTV supports conditional requests.
  • Management API remains authenticated.

docs.title: Reference Upgrade Failure
docs.text:
Assume:

  • Current release is healthy.
  • New release contains a database migration.
  • Migration fails validation.

Expected behavior:

  • Readiness remains false.
  • Application does not accept normal writes.
  • Pre-migration backup remains available.
  • Current database is preserved.
  • Logs identify migration ID.
  • Operator restores backup and starts prior image.
  • No automatic destructive downgrade runs.

docs.title: Reference Missing Key
docs.text:
Assume:

  • Durable database exists.
  • Master key file was not mounted.
  • Encrypted Media Source credentials exist.

Expected behavior:

  • ChannelForge does not generate a replacement key.
  • Readiness fails or recovery mode starts.
  • Logs state that the configured key is unavailable.
  • Secret values remain encrypted.
  • Operator remounts the original key.
  • Normal startup then continues.

docs.title: Version 1 Required Behaviors
docs.text:
The version 1 deployment must:

  1. Provide an official Docker image.
  2. Support Docker Compose.
  3. Support Unraid deployment.
  4. Run as non-root where practical.
  5. Preserve state in mounted storage.
  6. Use SQLite on supported local storage.
  7. Separate durable and temporary data.
  8. Support mounted secret key material.
  9. Report application and FFmpeg versions.
  10. Support configurable HTTP port.
  11. Support explicit public base URL.
  12. Support reverse proxies.
  13. Protect trusted forwarded headers.
  14. Support optional HDHomeRun-compatible discovery.
  15. Support manual tuner configuration without discovery.
  16. Support optional Intel or VA-API acceleration.
  17. Support optional NVIDIA acceleration when image and host permit.
  18. Support software fallback.
  19. Enforce resource admission.
  20. Provide liveness and readiness.
  21. Perform controlled startup reconciliation.
  22. Handle graceful shutdown.
  23. Run database migrations safely.
  24. Create migration backups according to policy.
  25. Support controlled upgrades.
  26. Document rollback.
  27. Support internal backup and restore.
  28. Provide structured logs.
  29. Provide support bundles with redaction.
  30. Avoid privileged mode.
  31. Avoid Docker socket access.
  32. Support read-only media mounts.
  33. Document storage and networking requirements.
  34. Support air-gapped local operation.
  35. Remain operable as one application container.

docs.title: Deployment Invariants
docs.text:
1. Durable state is not stored only in the container writable layer.
  2. Container recreation with the same durable storage preserves the instance.
  3. Container recreation does not create a new master key.
  4. Missing master key does not trigger silent replacement.
  5. SQLite uses a supported filesystem.
  6. Copying only a live main database file is not considered a verified backup.
  7. Migrations complete before readiness.
  8. Failed migration prevents normal startup.
  9. Pre-migration backup is preserved after failure.
  10. Normal deployment does not require root.
  11. Normal deployment does not require privileged mode.
  12. Normal deployment does not require Docker socket access.
  13. Media mounts may remain read-only.
  14. Device access is explicit.
  15. Public exposure is explicit.
  16. Trusted proxy headers are accepted only from trusted proxies.
  17. Stream proxy buffering is disabled where required.
  18. Public base URL controls generated external links.
  19. Discovery is configurable and not required for M3U use.
  20. Liveness does not depend on external Media Sources.
  21. Readiness depends on database and critical startup state.
  22. Graceful shutdown marks the service unready before stopping.
  23. Force termination is reconciled on next startup.
  24. Temporary file loss does not delete authoritative schedules.
  25. Last valid artifacts remain durable.
  26. Backup archives are verified.
  27. Restore activates only staged and verified data.
  28. Support bundles exclude secrets.
  29. Logs exclude secret values.
  30. Image version and revision are observable.
  31. Release images use pinned dependency resolution.
  32. Upgrades preserve durable storage.
  33. Downgrades do not run against unsupported newer schemas.
  34. Unraid and Compose represent the same persistence model.
  35. Version 1 does not require an external database or queue.

docs.title: ChannelForge Testing Specification
docs.text:
• Specification version: 0.1
  • Status: Draft
  • Last updated: 2026-07-27

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This document defines the ChannelForge testing architecture.

It specifies:

  • Test strategy
  • Deterministic testing
  • Unit testing
  • Component testing
  • Integration testing
  • Contract testing
  • End-to-end testing
  • Platform testing
  • Provider compatibility testing
  • SQLite testing
  • FFmpeg testing
  • Playout testing
  • Scheduling testing
  • API testing
  • Plugin testing
  • Security testing
  • Deployment testing
  • Migration testing
  • Backup and restore testing
  • Performance testing
  • Reliability testing
  • Fault injection
  • Test fixtures
  • Test data management
  • Test environments
  • Continuous integration
  • Release gates
  • Flaky-test policy
  • Coverage expectations
  • Test observability
  • Defect reproduction
  • Long-running validation

This document defines how ChannelForge proves that its architecture behaves as specified.

It does not define:

  • Exact test framework syntax
  • Exact CI vendor configuration
  • Exact test file names
  • Exact production monitoring thresholds
  • Exact release cadence
  • Exact implementation language
  • Exact code coverage tool

Those choices must satisfy the requirements defined here.

docs.title: Testing Mission
docs.text:
ChannelForge must prove that it can build television networks deterministically, play them reliably, survive failures, preserve state, and remain portable across supported deployment environments.

Testing must:

  • Verify domain invariants
  • Verify deterministic schedule generation
  • Verify persistence safety
  • Verify provider isolation
  • Verify stream continuity
  • Verify output compatibility
  • Verify security boundaries
  • Verify upgrade and restore behavior
  • Verify Docker and Unraid deployment
  • Verify supported CPU architectures
  • Detect platform-specific defects
  • Produce reproducible failures
  • Avoid hidden dependence on wall clock or network availability
  • Separate authoritative release gates from optional compatibility tests
  • Prevent flaky tests from becoming accepted noise

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Version 1 testing covers:

  • Core domain
  • Catalog normalization
  • Scheduling
  • Playout
  • Output generation
  • Plex integration
  • Jellyfin integration
  • Emby integration
  • SQLite persistence
  • REST API
  • Authentication and authorization
  • Plugin architecture
  • Docker images
  • Docker Compose
  • Unraid template
  • FFmpeg
  • Hardware acceleration where infrastructure permits
  • Backup and restore
  • Migration from inherited Tunarr state
  • Windows development behavior
  • Linux production behavior
  • amd64
  • arm64 where officially supported

docs.title: Testing Principles
docs.text:
1. Determinism is tested explicitly.
  2. Domain behavior is tested without infrastructure where possible.
  3. Infrastructure behavior is tested against real infrastructure where needed.
  4. Provider tests use fixtures and contract servers.
  5. Real provider tests are supplemental, not the only verification.
  6. Release gates run on Linux.
  7. Windows tests remain useful but do not override Linux production truth.
  8. A failing authoritative test blocks release.
  9. Flaky tests are defects.
  10. Test data is versioned.
  11. Time is controlled.
  12. Randomness is seeded.
  13. Ordering is explicit.
  14. External calls are mocked only at defined boundaries.
  15. Failure behavior is as important as success behavior.
  16. Migrations are tested with realistic prior data.
  17. Backups are tested by restore.
  18. Stream tests inspect actual media behavior.
  19. Security tests verify absence of leakage.
  20. Test results are observable and attributable.

docs.title: Test Pyramid
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    E2E["End-to-End and Platform Tests"]
    Integration["Integration and Contract Tests"]
    Component["Component and Service Tests"]
    Unit["Unit and Domain Tests"]

    E2E --> Integration
    Integration --> Component
    Component --> Unit

The largest test count should exist at the unit and component layers.

End-to-end tests should remain smaller, high-value, and stable.

docs.title: Unit Tests
docs.text: Unit tests verify one pure or narrowly scoped unit.

docs.title: Domain Tests
docs.text: Domain tests verify aggregate behavior and invariants without persistence or network dependencies.

docs.title: Component Tests
docs.text: Component tests verify one application module with controlled dependencies.

docs.title: Integration Tests
docs.text: Integration tests verify real collaboration between modules or infrastructure.

docs.title: Contract Tests
docs.text: Contract tests verify one side of a stable interface.

docs.title: End-to-End Tests
docs.text: End-to-end tests verify complete workflows through public interfaces.

docs.title: Platform Tests
docs.text: Platform tests verify supported operating systems, architectures, containers, filesystems, devices, and networking.

docs.title: Compatibility Tests
docs.text: Compatibility tests verify external clients, providers, and inherited behavior.

docs.title: Performance Tests
docs.text: Performance tests measure capacity, latency, throughput, and resource use.

docs.title: Reliability Tests
docs.text: Reliability tests verify recovery, fault containment, and long-running behavior.

docs.title: Authoritative Test Environments
docs.text:
The authoritative production-like environment is:

  • Linux container
  • Supported Docker Engine
  • SQLite on local supported storage
  • Bundled or supported FFmpeg
  • Supported Node.js runtime
  • Same application build used for release

docs.title: Windows Test Role
docs.text:
Windows is a supported development environment.

Windows tests verify:

  • Build
  • Type checking
  • Pure domain tests
  • API component tests where platform-neutral
  • PowerShell workflows
  • Path handling
  • Line-ending safety
  • Repository scripts
  • Documentation commands

Windows is not the authority for:

  • Linux path semantics
  • Container devices
  • Linux FFmpeg hardware access
  • POSIX file locking
  • Unraid behavior
  • Docker host networking
  • Linux signal handling

docs.title: Known Windows-Specific Test Classes
docs.text:
Expected Windows-specific differences may include:

  • Path separator assertions
  • Drive-letter paths
  • File-lock timing
  • SQLite temporary database cleanup
  • EBUSY behavior
  • Symlink permissions
  • Signal behavior
  • Docker networking
  • Shell command availability

A known platform difference must be documented and isolated.

It must not be hidden through broad test exclusion.

docs.title: Linux Release Authority
docs.text:
The Linux release suite must pass before release.

It includes:

  • Build
  • Type checking
  • Unit tests
  • Domain tests
  • Component tests
  • Integration tests
  • SQLite tests
  • API contract tests
  • Security tests
  • Docker image tests
  • Migration tests
  • Backup and restore tests
  • Stream smoke tests
  • Output validation

docs.title: Architecture Matrix
docs.text:
Supported test matrix may include:

linux/amd64
linux/arm64
windows/amd64 development

arm64 becomes a release gate only when officially supported.

docs.title: Test Determinism
docs.text:
Deterministic tests produce the same result from the same inputs.

Determinism applies to:

  • Schedule Plans
  • Catalog normalization
  • Matching
  • Rule evaluation
  • Candidate ordering
  • Random selection
  • Guide output
  • M3U output
  • API pagination
  • Projection rebuild
  • Migration result
  • Plugin rule behavior
  • Artifact checksums

docs.title: Sources of Nondeterminism
docs.text:
Common sources include:

  • Wall clock
  • Time zone
  • Daylight-saving transition
  • Random number generator
  • Database row order
  • Hash-map iteration
  • Concurrent completion order
  • External provider changes
  • Network latency
  • File enumeration order
  • Locale
  • Floating-point arithmetic
  • Process IDs
  • Temporary paths
  • UUID generation
  • Platform path separators

Tests must control or normalize these inputs.

docs.title: Controlled Clock
docs.text:
Application code should depend on a Clock abstraction for testable time.

Tests may set:

  • Current UTC instant
  • Local time zone
  • Clock progression
  • Clock rollback
  • Clock jump
  • Monotonic duration

docs.title: Time Zone Fixtures
docs.text:
Required time-zone cases include:

  • UTC
  • America/Los_Angeles
  • America/New_York
  • Europe/London
  • A zone without daylight saving
  • A zone with half-hour offset
  • A zone with historical transition where relevant

docs.title: Daylight-Saving Tests
docs.text:
Tests must cover:

  • Spring-forward missing local time
  • Fall-back repeated local time
  • Schedule horizon crossing transition
  • Recurring local anchor
  • Guide timestamps
  • Runtime instant lookup
  • Backup naming
  • Token expiration

docs.title: Seeded Randomness
docs.text:
Schedule generation and any randomized selection use explicit seeds.

Tests record:

  • Seed
  • Generator version
  • Rule versions
  • Input snapshot
  • Expected checksum

docs.title: Golden Determinism Test
docs.text:
A golden determinism test should:

  1. Load fixed Catalog Snapshot.
  2. Load fixed Programming Configuration Revision.
  3. Set fixed horizon.
  4. Set fixed time zone.
  5. Set fixed seed.
  6. Generate plan.
  7. Validate plan.
  8. Serialize canonical plan.
  9. Compare checksum or golden fixture.
  10. Repeat generation and compare exact output.

docs.title: Golden Fixture Policy
docs.text:
Golden fixtures are appropriate for:

  • Canonical schedule serialization
  • XMLTV
  • M3U
  • Provider normalization
  • API examples
  • Migration output
  • Plugin manifests
  • Error payloads

Golden fixtures must not hide unintended change.

Updating a golden requires review of the semantic difference.

docs.title: Canonical Serialization
docs.text:
Golden tests require stable serialization.

Canonicalization must define:

  • Field order
  • Collection order
  • Timestamp precision
  • Null handling
  • Numeric formatting
  • Newline style
  • Unicode normalization

docs.title: Randomized Property Testing
docs.text:
Property tests may generate many valid inputs while preserving reproducibility.

Every failure records the random seed.

docs.title: Test IDs
docs.text:
Long-running or generated tests should emit:

  • Test name
  • Seed
  • Fixture version
  • Platform
  • Application revision
  • Dependency versions

docs.title: Unit Testing
docs.text:
Unit tests should be:

  • Fast
  • Isolated
  • Deterministic
  • Independent of network
  • Independent of real clock
  • Independent of filesystem where possible
  • Easy to diagnose

docs.title: Unit Test Subjects
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Value objects
  • Identifier validation
  • Duration arithmetic
  • Time-zone conversion
  • Rule evaluation
  • Candidate scoring
  • Tie-breaking
  • Error mapping
  • URL validation
  • Path mapping
  • Permission evaluation
  • Retry classification
  • Cursor encoding
  • ETag generation
  • Redaction
  • Manifest validation

docs.title: Domain Aggregate Tests
docs.text:
Every aggregate should test:

  • Creation
  • Valid mutation
  • Invalid mutation
  • Version change
  • Archival
  • Restoration
  • Immutable state
  • Event emission
  • Invariant protection
  • Concurrency expectation

docs.title: Network Aggregate Tests
docs.text:
Test:

  • Create Network
  • Add Channel
  • Remove Channel
  • Activate Network Profile Revision
  • Archive Network
  • Restore Network
  • Prevent invalid active revision
  • Preserve Channel identity

docs.title: Channel Aggregate Tests
docs.text:
Test:

  • Create Channel
  • Assign channel number
  • Change display name
  • Change time zone
  • Activate programming revision
  • Publish approved plan
  • Archive
  • Restore
  • Reject invalid publication
  • Compare-and-swap publication

docs.title: Revision Tests
docs.text:
Test:

  • Draft creation
  • Draft editing
  • Validation
  • Approval
  • Superseding
  • Approved immutability
  • Checksum stability
  • Version conflict

docs.title: Catalog Domain Tests
docs.text:
Test:

  • Catalog Item creation
  • Source Binding association
  • Playback Variant association
  • Metadata provenance
  • Effective metadata selection
  • User override
  • Merge
  • Split
  • Archive
  • Restoration
  • Availability
  • Snapshot creation

docs.title: Schedule Plan Domain Tests
docs.text:
Test:

  • Plan creation
  • Entry order
  • Positive durations
  • No gap where continuous coverage required
  • No overlap
  • Carry-In
  • Carry-Out
  • Approval
  • Rejection
  • Publication eligibility
  • Immutable entries
  • Lineage
  • Staleness

docs.title: Component Testing
docs.text:
Component tests verify a module through its public application interface.

Examples:

  • Catalog synchronization service
  • Schedule generation service
  • Publication service
  • Playout decision service
  • Backup service
  • Plugin lifecycle service
  • Authentication service

docs.title: Component Test Dependencies
docs.text:
Use:

  • In-memory fakes for stable ports
  • Temporary SQLite when persistence semantics matter
  • Recorded provider fixtures
  • Fake clock
  • Seeded random source
  • Fake secret broker
  • Fake file storage
  • Mock FFmpeg supervisor

docs.title: Mocking Policy
docs.text:
Mocks should verify interaction only when interaction is the contract.

Avoid mocking every internal method.

Prefer:

  • Fakes
  • Test repositories
  • Contract servers
  • Real SQLite
  • Real serialization

docs.title: Boundary Mocking
docs.text:
Mock at:

  • External provider HTTP boundary
  • FFmpeg process boundary
  • Secret store boundary
  • Operating-system device boundary
  • Clock
  • Random source
  • Notification delivery
  • Plugin process boundary

docs.title: Over-Mocking Risk
docs.text:
A test that replaces:

  • Repository mapping
  • Domain validation
  • Serialization
  • API schema
  • Provider mapping

with mocks may pass while the real integration fails.

docs.title: Integration Testing
docs.text: Integration tests use real implementations of multiple modules.

docs.title: Integration Test Categories
docs.text:
• Application plus SQLite
  • Adapter plus mock provider server
  • API plus application services
  • Artifact generator plus managed storage
  • FFmpeg supervisor plus real FFmpeg
  • Plugin broker plus isolated test plugin
  • Backup service plus filesystem
  • Restore service plus migration
  • Docker image plus health endpoint

docs.title: Temporary Database
docs.text:
Integration tests should use isolated temporary SQLite databases.

Each test or suite must avoid state leakage.

docs.title: SQLite Test Cleanup
docs.text:
Cleanup must:

  • Close connections
  • Release prepared statements
  • Stop jobs
  • Remove WAL and shared-memory files
  • Retry bounded cleanup on Windows
  • Report leaked handles

docs.title: SQLite File Naming
docs.text:
Use unique deterministic or random test paths.

The path should include:

  • Test run ID
  • Test suite
  • Process identity where necessary

docs.title: SQLite In-Memory Mode
docs.text:
In-memory SQLite is useful for some tests.

It is insufficient for:

  • WAL
  • File locking
  • Backup
  • Restore
  • Crash recovery
  • Multi-connection behavior
  • Filesystem permission
  • Disk-full simulation

docs.title: SQLite Integration Matrix
docs.text:
Test:

  • In-memory database
  • Temporary file database
  • WAL mode
  • Non-WAL mode if supported
  • Multiple readers
  • Competing writers
  • Busy timeout
  • Foreign keys
  • Migration
  • Backup
  • Restore
  • Integrity checks

docs.title: SQLite Concurrency Tests
docs.text:
Required scenarios:

  • Reader during writer
  • Two writers
  • Long reader
  • Busy timeout
  • Retry success
  • Retry exhaustion
  • Optimistic conflict
  • Background synchronization versus publication
  • Backup during reads
  • Backup during bounded writes

docs.title: SQLite Windows Behavior
docs.text:
Windows integration tests should specifically test:

  • Closing all connections
  • Deleting database
  • Deleting WAL
  • Deleting shared-memory file
  • Retry on EBUSY
  • Antivirus-induced delay where reproducible

Known Windows cleanup instability must not weaken Linux release tests.

docs.title: Repository Contract Tests
docs.text:
Every repository implementation must satisfy a shared contract.

Contract categories:

  • Create
  • Read
  • Update
  • Archive
  • Restore
  • List
  • Stable ordering
  • Pagination
  • Concurrency
  • Unique constraint
  • Foreign-key constraint
  • Transaction rollback

docs.title: Provider Contract Testing
docs.text: Built-in adapters require provider contract suites.

docs.title: Provider Test Server
docs.text:
A provider test server should emulate:

  • Authentication
  • Server identity
  • Library listing
  • Item listing
  • Item details
  • Pagination
  • Artwork
  • Playback info
  • Errors
  • Timeouts
  • Rate limiting
  • Version differences
  • Webhooks where applicable

docs.title: Recorded Fixture Policy
docs.text:
Provider fixtures may be:

  • Synthetic
  • Sanitized recorded responses
  • Hand-authored edge cases

Fixtures must contain no real credentials or personal data.

docs.title: Provider Fixture Metadata
docs.text:
Each fixture records:

  • Provider
  • Provider version
  • Endpoint
  • Scenario
  • Sanitization version
  • Fixture schema version
  • Expected normalized result

docs.title: Plex Test Coverage
docs.text:
Plex adapter tests must cover:

  • Valid token
  • Invalid token
  • Server identity
  • Library sections
  • Movie library
  • TV library
  • Mixed or unsupported library
  • Movie metadata
  • Series metadata
  • Season metadata
  • Episode metadata
  • Media parts
  • Multiple versions
  • Artwork
  • Provider IDs
  • Missing parent
  • Missing duration
  • Playback URL resolution
  • Direct stream
  • Provider transcode
  • Redirect
  • Timeout
  • Rate limiting
  • Malformed response
  • Provider version variation

docs.title: Jellyfin Test Coverage
docs.text:
Jellyfin adapter tests must cover:

  • Valid API key or token
  • Invalid credential
  • Server identity
  • User identity
  • Virtual folders
  • Movie library
  • TV library
  • Movie metadata
  • Series hierarchy
  • Media Sources
  • Media Streams
  • PlaybackInfo

  • Pagination

docs.title: Emby Test Coverage
docs.text:
Emby adapter tests must cover:

  • Valid token
  • Invalid token
  • Server identity
  • User scope
  • Libraries
  • Movie metadata
  • Series hierarchy
  • Media Sources
  • Media Streams
  • Playback resolution
  • Artwork
  • Permission change
  • Missing item
  • Pagination
  • Provider version variation
  • Timeout
  • Rate limiting
  • Malformed response

docs.title: Provider Identity Replacement Test
docs.text:
Test:

  1. Configure source against provider identity A.
  2. Synchronize.
  3. Change test server identity to B.
  4. Run connection probe.
  5. Verify mismatch.
  6. Verify synchronization block.
  7. Verify existing bindings remain attached to A.
  8. Verify audit finding.

docs.title: Provider Permission Change Test
docs.text:
Test:

  1. Synchronize visible libraries.
  2. Remove provider permission.
  3. Return fewer items.
  4. Run incremental synchronization.
  5. Verify no immediate destructive deletion.
  6. Queue full reconciliation.
  7. Apply grace policy.

docs.title: Provider Cursor Tests
docs.text:
Test:

  • Initial cursor
  • Next cursor
  • Cursor resume
  • Expired cursor
  • Invalid cursor
  • Adapter version change
  • Full reconciliation fallback

docs.title: Real Provider Compatibility Tests
docs.text:
Optional controlled tests may run against real:

  • Plex
  • Jellyfin
  • Emby

They are supplemental because:

  • Versions change
  • Setup is expensive
  • Network may fail
  • Data may vary
  • Credentials are sensitive

docs.title: Real Provider Test Requirements
docs.text:
• Dedicated test server
  • Dedicated credential
  • Synthetic library
  • Known media files
  • Recorded provider version
  • No personal data
  • No production mutation
  • Secret handling
  • Cleanup
  • Skippable outside compatibility environment

docs.title: Provider Compatibility Report
docs.text:
A compatibility run should report:

  • Provider version
  • Server platform
  • Authentication mode
  • Libraries
  • Item count
  • Playback mode
  • Passed scenarios
  • Failed scenarios
  • Warnings
  • ChannelForge revision

docs.title: Catalog Synchronization Testing
docs.text:
Test modes:

  • Initial

  • Incremental
  • Targeted item
  • Webhook-triggered
  • Resume
  • Cancellation
  • Source disable
  • Library exclusion
  • Provider outage

docs.title: Catalog Batch Tests
docs.text:
Verify:

  • Bounded batch size
  • Transaction commit
  • Checkpoint update
  • Failure rollback
  • Next page outside transaction
  • Duplicate item idempotency
  • Provenance
  • Variant update
  • Missing reconciliation only after completion

docs.title: Catalog Matching Tests
docs.text:
Test:

  • Title and year candidate
  • Series hierarchy
  • Duplicate movie
  • Multiple cuts
  • Ambiguous match
  • User override
  • Merge
  • Split
  • Provider ID conflict

docs.title: Catalog Golden Fixtures
docs.text:
Golden normalized Catalog Items should cover:

  • Movie
  • Series
  • Season
  • Episode
  • Special
  • Multiple versions
  • Multi-part file
  • Missing metadata
  • Conflicting metadata
  • Archived source
  • Unavailable source

docs.title: Scheduling Test Architecture
docs.text: Scheduling is one of the highest-risk deterministic subsystems.

docs.title: Scheduling Test Classes
docs.text:
• Rule unit tests
  • Candidate selection tests
  • Block placement tests
  • Daypart tests
  • Rotation tests
  • Repeat-window tests
  • Marathon tests
  • Episode ordering tests
  • Filler tests
  • Alignment tests
  • Regeneration tests
  • Locked-entry tests
  • Plan validation tests
  • Determinism tests
  • Scale tests

docs.title: Schedule Input Fixture
docs.text:
A complete schedule fixture includes:

  • Catalog Snapshot
  • Network Profile Revision
  • Programming Configuration Revision
  • Channel time zone
  • Horizon
  • Seed
  • Generator version
  • Rule versions
  • Prior plan where applicable
  • Locked entries
  • Maintenance intervals
  • Expected warnings

docs.title: Schedule Output Verification
docs.text:
Verify:

  • Coverage
  • No illegal gaps
  • No illegal overlaps
  • Entry sequence
  • Duration conservation
  • Rule evidence
  • Hard-rule compliance
  • Soft-rule scoring
  • Repeat windows
  • Episode sequence
  • Block boundaries
  • Daypart boundaries
  • Carry-In and Carry-Out
  • Guide snapshot
  • Checksum

docs.title: Hard Rule Tests
docs.text:
A hard rule violation must:

  • Exclude candidate
  • Produce evidence
  • Fail generation when no legal candidate exists
  • Never silently become a soft penalty

docs.title: Soft Rule Tests
docs.text:
A soft rule must:

  • Produce deterministic score
  • Use fixed-point or stable arithmetic
  • Produce explanation
  • Respect priority and weight
  • Avoid affecting hard eligibility

docs.title: Tie-Breaking Tests
docs.text:
Tie-breaking must be explicit.

Test:

  • Equal score
  • Equal duration
  • Equal metadata
  • Stable ID tie-break
  • Seeded random tie-break where intended
  • Database order changes

docs.title: Repeat Window Tests
docs.text:
Test:

  • Exact boundary
  • Just inside window
  • Just outside window
  • Series-level repeat
  • Episode-level repeat
  • Franchise-level repeat
  • Historical airing input
  • Regenerated range

docs.title: Episode Ordering Tests
docs.text:
Test:

  • Air-date order
  • Season and episode order
  • Specials
  • Missing episode number
  • Multi-episode files
  • User-defined order
  • Restart behavior
  • Skipped unavailable episode

docs.title: Block Tests
docs.text:
Test:

  • Fixed block
  • Flexible block
  • Nested segment if supported
  • Overrun
  • Underrun
  • Filler
  • Boundary alignment
  • Locked block
  • Regeneration around block

docs.title: Daypart Tests
docs.text:
Test:

  • Local-time daypart
  • Midnight crossing
  • DST transition
  • Overlapping dayparts
  • Missing daypart
  • Priority resolution
  • Weekend
  • Holiday if supported

docs.title: Filler Tests
docs.text:
Test:

  • Exact-fit filler
  • Short filler
  • Multiple fillers
  • No filler
  • Maximum filler chain
  • Filler repeat
  • Presentation asset
  • Dead air policy

docs.title: Regeneration Tests
docs.text:
Test:

  • Full regeneration
  • Range regeneration
  • Preserve locked entries
  • Preserve outside range
  • Carry-In continuity
  • Carry-Out continuity
  • Seed behavior
  • Staleness
  • Approval invalidation
  • Lineage

docs.title: Schedule Validation Tests
docs.text:
Validate:

  • Entry duration
  • Entry order
  • Timeline continuity
  • Catalog availability
  • Rule compliance
  • Asset availability
  • Guide data
  • Publication eligibility
  • Warning acknowledgement
  • Horizon requirements

docs.title: Schedule Snapshot Tests
docs.text:
A Catalog Snapshot used for generation must remain immutable.

Test that later Catalog changes do not alter a previously generated plan.

docs.title: Schedule Scale Tests
docs.text:
Test representative sizes:

  • 1 Channel, 1 day
  • 1 Channel, 7 days
  • 10 Channels, 7 days

docs.title: Playout Testing
docs.text: Playout tests verify actual runtime behavior.

docs.title: Playout Test Layers
docs.text:
• Decision unit tests
  • Session component tests

  • Stream protocol tests
  • Client compatibility tests
  • Long-running soak tests

docs.title: Playout Decision Tests
docs.text:
Test:

  • Variant selection
  • Stream mode
  • Hardware selection

  • Retry
  • Fallback
  • Maintenance content

docs.title: Runtime Offset Tests
docs.text:
Test:

docs.title: Source Selection Tests

  • Late join

docs.title: FFmpeg Test Harness
docs.text:
The FFmpeg harness should:

docs.title: Synthetic Media Fixtures
docs.text:
Create versioned fixtures for:

  • H.264/AAC MP4
  • H.265/AAC
  • MPEG-2 transport stream

docs.text:
Test media must be:

docs.title: Media Fixture Checksums
docs.text:
Every media fixture has:

  • Checksum

docs.title: FFprobe Verification
docs.text:
Use FFprobe or equivalent to verify:

  • Container
  • Streams

  • Resolution

  10. Verify Catalog.
  11. Verify Schedule Plan.
  12. Verify XMLTV.
  13. Verify M3U.
  14. Verify stream.
  15. Verify plugin state.

docs.text:

docs.title: Test Fixtures
docs.text: Fixtures are versioned project assets.

docs.title: Fixture Categories
docs.text:
• Catalog
  • Provider
  • Schedule
  • Media
  • Database
  • Plugin
  • API
  • Security
  • Deployment
  • Backup
  • XMLTV

docs.title: Fixture Directory Principles
docs.text:
Fixtures should be:

  • Discoverable
  • Named by scenario
  • Immutable after release use
  • Small where possible
  • Sanitized
  • Licensed
  • Checksum protected
  • Documented

docs.title: Fixture Versioning
docs.text: A breaking fixture change creates a new fixture version.

docs.title: Fixture Generators
docs.text:
Generated fixtures must be reproducible.

Record generator version and seed.

docs.title: Synthetic Catalog Generator
docs.text:
A synthetic catalog generator may produce:

  • Movies
  • Series
  • Seasons
  • Episodes
  • Specials
  • Multiple versions
  • Missing metadata
  • Conflicts
  • Different durations
  • Genres
  • Ratings
  • Availability

docs.title: Synthetic Provider Server
docs.text: A synthetic provider server may expose selectable scenarios through fixed configuration.

docs.title: Secret Sentinels
docs.text:
Security tests should use distinctive sentinel secrets.

Example categories:

  • TEST_PROVIDER_TOKEN_...
  • TEST_PLUGIN_SECRET_...
  • TEST_STREAM_KEY_...

They must never resemble production credentials.

docs.title: Test Data Privacy
docs.text: No real user data should enter the repository or ordinary CI artifacts.

docs.title: Sanitization
docs.text:
Recorded provider payloads must remove:

  • Usernames
  • Emails
  • Tokens
  • IP addresses
  • Library names where sensitive
  • File paths
  • Device IDs where sensitive
  • Viewing history

docs.title: Test Database Privacy
docs.text: Migration fixtures must use synthetic data.

docs.title: Test Isolation
docs.text: Tests must not share mutable state unless the suite explicitly coordinates it.

docs.title: Port Allocation
docs.text:
Network tests should use:

  • Dynamically allocated ports
  • Reserved test ranges
  • Conflict detection
  • Cleanup

docs.title: Process Cleanup
docs.text:
Every test launching a process must:

  • Track process
  • Apply timeout
  • Terminate on failure
  • Wait for exit
  • Capture bounded logs
  • Report leak

docs.title: File Cleanup
docs.text:
Every test creating files must:

  • Use isolated root
  • Clean on success
  • Preserve on failure only when configured
  • Retry bounded cleanup
  • Report leftovers

docs.title: Test Timeouts
docs.text:
Every asynchronous test needs a timeout.

Timeout values should be:

  • Long enough for expected environment
  • Short enough to detect hang
  • Different by test tier
  • Recorded in failure output

docs.title: Retry Policy for Tests
docs.text:
Authoritative tests should not be retried automatically to turn failure into success.

A retry may be used only to diagnose flakiness and must preserve the first failure.

docs.title: Flaky Test Policy
docs.text:
A flaky test is one that produces inconsistent results without code change.

Flaky tests are defects.

docs.title: Flaky Test Handling
docs.text:
When detected:

  1. Record failure evidence.
  2. Create issue.
  3. Identify owner.
  4. Quarantine only if it blocks unrelated work.
  5. Preserve a separate required signal where possible.
  6. Set expiration for quarantine.
  7. Fix root cause.
  8. Restore to authoritative suite.

docs.title: Quarantined Test
docs.text:
A quarantined test:

  • Still runs in a nonblocking job
  • Reports failures
  • Has issue reference
  • Has owner
  • Has expiration
  • Does not count as permanent coverage

docs.title: Prohibited Flake Practices
docs.text:
Do not:

  • Add arbitrary sleeps
  • Increase timeout without analysis
  • Retry until pass
  • Remove assertion
  • Ignore failure
  • Skip entire platform broadly
  • Depend on test order

docs.title: Flake Diagnostics
docs.text:
Capture:

  • Seed
  • Clock
  • Platform
  • CPU load
  • Memory
  • Port
  • Temp path
  • Logs
  • Process list
  • Database state
  • Provider scenario
  • Test duration

docs.title: Test Ordering
docs.text:
Tests must pass in:

  • Declared order
  • Randomized order where practical
  • Isolated execution
  • Parallel execution where supported

docs.title: Parallel Testing
docs.text:
Parallel tests must not share:

  • Port
  • Database
  • Temp path
  • Global clock
  • Environment mutation
  • Provider scenario
  • Plugin storage

docs.title: Serial Test Classification
docs.text:
Tests may be serial when they require:

  • Hardware device
  • Host network
  • Global resource
  • Migration fixture mutation
  • Fixed external client
  • Resource-intensive soak

Serial classification must be explicit.

docs.title: Continuous Integration
docs.text: CI should provide fast feedback and authoritative release confidence.

docs.title: CI Stages
docs.text:
Suggested stages:

  1. Repository validation
  2. Formatting and lint
  3. Type checking
  4. Unit and domain tests
  5. Component tests
  6. Integration tests
  7. API and security tests
  8. Build
  9. Docker image test
  10. Migration test
  11. Stream smoke test
  12. Platform matrix
  13. Artifact publication
  14. Scheduled compatibility and soak

docs.title: Pull Request Gate
docs.text:
A pull request gate should require:
